10587-the-poetical-works-of-addison-gay-:
Rev. George Gilfillan edited this 1859 volume of poetry by Joseph Addison, with Gay's Fables and Somerville's Chase. Gilfillan adds memoirs and critical dissertations, placing each poet in his age. Addison, the Spectator essayist, appears here as a poet of occasions, translations, and odes.

Poems to Dryden, to his Majesty, a translation of Virgil's Fourth Georgic, songs for St. Cecilia's Day, and a letter from Italy fill Addison's section. Gay's fables and Somerville's hunting poem follow. Readers get a solid, Victorian-era collection of Augustan verse, useful for students of English poetry.
1145-rupert-of-hentzau-from-the-memoirs-:
Anthony Hope brings back Rudolf Rassendyll, the Englishman who once stood in for the King of Ruritania, for a darker sequel. Rupert of Hentzau, the dashing villain who escaped last time, plots murder and blackmail, and Rassendyll must return in disguise to save the queen and the throne.

The tale moves through duels, letters, and midnight meetings, with Fritz von Tarlenheim narrating. Hope writes the romance at a gallop, and the ending is more tragic than the first book's. The sequel keeps the Ruritania myth alive, and it still delights swashbuckler fans.
11572-the-man-from-brodney-s:
George Barr McCutcheon's 1908 novel opens with the late Mister Skaggs, an extraordinary document, and the arrival of Hollingsworth Chase. English visitors invade a château, and the Brownes arrive soon after, setting a social comedy in motion. Chase, the man from Brodney's, must face an enemy across house and grounds.

Later chapters bring an American bar, a slough of tranquillity, and women and women as a theme. Chase performs a miracle, a lantern hangs above, and a plan from Mister Saunders takes shape. A burning bungalow, a plague announced, and a charity ball close the middle of the tale, with romance and intrigue throughout.
11698-the-three-bronte-s:
May Sinclair's 1912 study of the three Brontës draws on Clement Shorter's copyright material, Emily Brontë's poems, and translations from St. John of the Cross. Her prefatory note thanks Shorter, Dodd and Mead, Hodder and Stoughton, and Arthur Symons for leave to quote.

Sinclair writes of Emily's immeasurable superiority to her sad sisters, and of Shirley, who could lie stirless on turf under a friendly tree, needing no society but the world around her. Appendices and an index close the book. The study is a modern critic's attempt to separate three sisters too often read as one.
12990-a-residence-in-france-with-an-excu:
James Fenimore Cooper's Residence in France, with an excursion up the Rhine and a second visit to Switzerland, appeared in Paris in 1836. Cooper first visited Switzerland in 1828 and returned in 1832, finding nature unchanged but European politics transformed. A long digression on another country's situation, the preface warns, will interrupt the travel tale.

Church carving draws Cooper's eye: a Brussels pulpit shows the Conversion of St. Paul, horse and rider larger than life, while wooden figures over a hospital door at Gorcum or Breda outshine pretentious statuary. The book blends travel, art, and political comment. It shows Cooper the observer abroad, not only the novelist of the frontier.
13588-the-young-gentleman-and-lady-s-mon:
J. Hamilton Moore, author of The Practical Navigator, gathers select pieces from the best modern writers for young gentlemen and ladies in this monitor and English teacher's assistant. The collection aims to root out vulgar prejudice and rusticity, improve understanding, rectify will, purify passions, and teach reading, writing, and speaking with elegance and propriety.

Divided into small portions for class reading, it suits schools, academies, and private readers who cannot buy the celebrated authors whole. A bad education is shown in an only son spoiled by fortune, while hurry is condemned as the mark of little minds, puzzled when they should be cool and deliberate. Moore's book is Georgian conduct teaching through anthology.
13891-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson compiled the messages and papers of the presidents, and this volume covers Theodore Roosevelt. It prints messages, proclamations, and executive orders to the end of the Fifty-seventh Congress, first session. A sketch introduces Roosevelt, twenty-seventh in Richardson's count, born in New York in 1858. His Harvard years and early travel follow.

The papers show Roosevelt meeting the people and facing the assassin who struck McKinley, his predecessor. Official prose records policy, appointments, and public grief in formal terms. Richardson's compilation aimed to give citizens the full presidential record. The volume serves historians of the Progressive Era. It also preserves Roosevelt's early presidential voice.
14584-a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-:
James D. Richardson's tenth volume of presidential messages and papers, published in 1902, closes a task begun in April 1895 that took more than four years. Richardson, a Tennessee representative, compiled the official papers of the presidents.

The volume's great labor was its index, mainly prepared by his son over three years, with every reference checked against the text. The papers themselves include Madison's 1812 messages to Congress on British agents and frontier troubles. The compilation remains a standard reference for American presidential documents. The index alone ran to hundreds of pages of cross references, and Richardson checked it himself.
14623-six-little-bunkers-at-grandma-bell:
Laura Lee Hope's Six Little Bunkers at Grandma Bell's, illustrated and published by Grosset and Dunlap, follows the six Bunker children to their grandmother's house. Hope also wrote the Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown series.

Russ, Rose, Vi, Laddie, Mun Bun, and Margy pack and watch the expressman load an auto truck. They count noses before Jerry Simms drives them off, only for Margy to go missing at the start. The children's mishaps and reunions fill the book. It is a cheerful early reader's novel, simple and kindly, for the youngest chapter-book audience.
14750-bowdoin-boys-in-labrador-an-accoun:
Jonathan Prince Cilley Jr. recounts the Bowdoin College scientific expedition to Labrador in 1891, led by Professor Leslie A. Lee of the biological department. The party sails in the Julia A. Decker, waiting out wind and fog at the Gut of Canso before pushing north.

On shore and aboard, the students measure, photograph and collect. Lee records heights, arm spans, head shapes and facial features among Micmac people met on the way, while the photographic corps preserves faces and dress. Natural history, camp routine and the slow work of field science fill a lively student journal of a summer at the edge of the known map.
15018-elements-of-civil-government-a-tex:
Alex. L. Peterman, late principal of a normal school, writes Elements of Civil Government as a textbook for public schools, high schools and normal schools, and as a manual of reference for teachers. Its contents run through seventeen chapters and more, covering the structure and work of government step by step.

Students learn how local, state and national government operate, what officers do, and how laws are made and carried out. Peterman writes plainly for classroom use, with questions and reference material for teachers. The book remains a clear example of early twentieth-century civics teaching: orderly, patriotic and meant to make young citizens understand the machinery they would one day use.
15151-a-book-of-the-play-studies-and-ill:
Dutton Cook's Book of the Play, in a third revised edition of 1881, studies stage life, story, and character without pretending to be a full history. Cook says he chose by-paths: details and curiosities of actors' lives, past and present, that grander chroniclers passed over. The first edition appeared in 1876.

Chapters collect anecdotes, stage customs, and portraits of players, offering entertainment as well as information. Cook writes for theatre lovers who enjoy backstage talk. Readers interested in Victorian stage history will find the book lively, gossipy, and full of detail larger histories miss.
16332-a-short-life-of-abraham-lincoln-co:
John G. Nicolay boiled down his vast multi-volume Lincoln history, written with John Hay, into this single readable life, issued in 1904. It follows Lincoln from a Kentucky birth and Indiana boyhood through New Salem, the Black Hawk War, law practice, and the long climb to the White House. Flatboat trips, storekeeping, and early votes all get their place.

The later chapters carry the story through the Civil War years that made Lincoln famous. Because Nicolay knew Lincoln and his papers at first hand, the account feels close and sure. For readers who want the full arc without the full shelf of volumes, this short life is a solid place to start.
17274-the-investment-of-influence-a-stud:
Newell Dwight Hillis's 1897 Investment of Influence, subtitled A Study of Social Sympathy and Service, argues that self-care must gain its complement in service to others. Chapters treat the atmosphere a person carries, great hearts and helpfulness, and the investment of talent and its return. Vicarious lives, genius and the debt of strength, and the supremacy of heart over brain follow. Renown through self-renunciation and silent fidelity close the moral arc.

Hillis writes in earnest, pulpit prose, with examples from field, forum, home, and market place. The book suits readers of Victorian self-help and social gospel thought. Its message, that influence is wealth to be spent on others, still speaks to anyone who wants a life that counts beyond itself.
17492-six-little-bunkers-at-cousin-tom-s:
Laura Lee Hope, author of the Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown series, published this children's book in 1918, with pictures. The six little Bunkers, led by Sammie, arrive at Cousin Tom's after a boat trip, a mix-up, and Margy's crawl. Sammie's story opens the book, treasure hopes follow, and digging for gold, Rose's locket, and a sand house keep the children busy.

Each chapter gives the young heroes a small adventure suited to their age, told in Hope's plain, kindly style. Readers get a gentle family story of cousins, summer days, and make-believe treasure hunting. The book belongs to the long run of early twentieth-century series fiction that kept children reading from one volume to the next.
17535-the-jester-of-st-timothy-s:
Arthur Stanwood Pier, author of Boys of St. Timothy's and Harding of St. Timothy's, published this school story in New York in 1911 with Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures. Chapters open with Irving setting forth on his adventure and achieving a name for himself. Westby's amusements, the baiting of a master, and master turned pupil follow.

The penalty for a foul, the worm beginning to turn, and the Harvard freshman carry Irving's school career on, with Westby in the game and master and boy ahead. Readers get a boys' school tale of wit, pluck, and fair play, in Pier's clean, popular style. The book suits readers of school stories.
17761-six-little-bunkers-at-grandpa-ford:
Laura Lee Hope, author of the Bunny Brown, Bobbsey Twins, and Outdoor Girls series, wrote this children's book of the six little Bunkers at Grandpa Ford's, with pictures. Chapters open with the man on the porch and Grandpa Ford himself, followed by something queer and Russ making a balloon. The big bang noise, off to Great Hedge, and Mun Bun taking something follow.

A big storm and a stay at Tarrington carry the visit on. Readers get a gentle family story of grandchildren, summer days, and small mishaps, in Hope's plain, kindly style. The book suits young readers who enjoy series stories of home and holiday.
17937-the-thin-santa-claus-the-chicken-y:
Ellis Parker Butler wrote this comic Christmas tale in 1909, with pictures by May Wilson Preston. It opens on a gray, drizzly Christmas morn, when Mrs. Gratz wakes, looks at the mud, and sighs that such weather must keep Santa Claus away from her house.

A thin man soon turns up in her chicken yard, hunting for germs and looking more like a man who lost nine hundred dollars than like Saint Nick. Butler plays the mix-up for laughs, with farm talk and dry wit. It is a short, funny holiday tale, best for readers who like a Santa story with a twist and a grin.
18371-giotto-and-his-works-in-padua-an-e:
John Ruskin wrote this explanatory notice of Giotto and his works in Padua, as part of his complete works issued by the National Library Association. The notice explains the series of woodcuts made for the Arundel Society after the frescoes in the Arena Chapel. Ruskin disclaims any attempt at a full life of Giotto, which would need a search through Italian libraries for documents of his working years.

Instead Ruskin collects, from published materials, what a viewer needs to read the frescoes: their subjects, order, and meaning in the chapel. The Arena Chapel series stands as Giotto's great narrative of the lives of Mary and Christ, told in color on plaster. Readers get Ruskin as guide: a critic standing before the walls at Padua, explaining picture by picture why Giotto changed the art of Europe.
18461-six-little-bunkers-at-mammy-june-s:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, with pictures by Walter S. Rogers. It belongs to the Six Little Bunkers series, alongside volumes at Grandma Bell's, Aunt Jo's, Cousin Tom's, and Cowboy Jack's, and to Hope's Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown books.

The story opens with Violet asking how William could get the croup, while Rose and Russ Bunker work on a cut-up puzzle. Later chapters carry the family south, with an Eskimo igloo and a snowman. A sea-eagle, a signal of distress, and a stay at Mammy June's plantation follow, where Christmas comes on the Fourth of July.
1939-a-gentleman-of-france-being-the-mem:
Stanley Weyman tells this tale as the memoirs of Gaston de Bonne, Sieur de Marsac, a gentleman of France in the wars of religion. The chapters open with the sport of fools and follow Gaston through duels, sieges, and court intrigues, with a hero who narrates his own adventures in the first person.

A scene in which Gaston pauses in shadow while a man might count ten, fixing in memory the position of a window, shows Weyman's method. Small, exact details make a romance feel real. The novel is a classic of the historical adventure, and its hero's honor, wit, and nerve carry a long story without flagging.
19561-the-outdoor-girls-in-a-motor-car-o:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this tale of the Outdoor Girls in a motor car, subtitled the haunted mansion of Shadow Valley, published in New York with pictures. Betty, Grace, and Mollie drive through fine country toward Wendell City, stopping so often for views that they fall far behind schedule.

Sun, dry roads, and a pleasant morning set them speeding onward again, toward the mansion that gives the book its mystery. The novel mixes motoring fun with a gentle ghost story, in the series' friendly style for girls. A queer peddler and a strange girl cross the tour, and Mr Lagg's offer sets the Shadow Valley trip in motion.
19702-the-rector-of-st-mark-s:
Mary J. Holmes wrote this novel of the rector of St. Mark's, published in Chicago. A young rector, his Sunday sermon done, turns gladly to a south window where June roses peep in, savoring the relief of a week's work finished.

Soon a handsome stranger comes up the garden walk, asking after Miss Henrietta Mayfield and pleading a suit with flurried haste. Holmes, a popular novelist of domestic romance, weaves church life, courtship, and small-town talk into a warm, old-fashioned tale. A wedding subplot has a groom object to bridesmaids in general, unless Fanny marries at the same time.
19736-six-little-bunkers-at-aunt-jo-s:
Laura Lee Hope was the shared pen name behind several children's series. Six Little Bunkers at Aunt Jo's, from 1918, follows the six Bunker children on a visit. Mother Bunker counts her children every time they leave the woods. She compares the habit to a soldier captain's muster. None of the six must be left behind.

The Bunkers were Russ, Laddie, Rose, Violet, Margy, and Mun Bun. Each book took them to a new relative or place. Small mishaps, lost toys, and mild scares fill their days. The counting joke shows the series' warm, busy tone. These books taught young readers chapter-book stamina. They also picture a large, cheerful American family of 1918.
19816-six-little-bunkers-at-cowboy-jack-:
Six Little Bunkers at Cowboy Jack's, from 1921, takes the Bunker family west. A September rain at the seashore opens the traveling. The children had never seen rain like the autumn equinox storms. Daddy Bunker and Captain Ben name the season for them. From shore the family journeys toward Cowboy Jack's ranch. Laura Lee Hope's series moved its six children like a touring company.

Each Bunkers book changed the setting and kept the family. Ranch life meant horses, wide weather, and new helpers. The six siblings split into pairs for small adventures. Young readers practiced chapters through gentle incident. Cowboy Jack's gave Eastern children a safe West. The series' warmth is its whole argument.
19849-flag-and-fleet-how-the-british-nav:
Flag and Fleet tells how the British Navy won the freedom of the seas. It was written for Canadian boys and girls. The Navy League of Canada sponsored its publication. Provincial education departments approved it for young readers. The dedication thanks a benefactor for kindnesses during the Great War. Sea power is its lesson from first page to last.

After 1918, Britain's navy seemed to have kept trade alive. Books like this taught imperial gratitude as history. Canadian children were the empire's audience and future sailors. William Wood, the naval historian, wrote in this vein often. Short chapters carry famous fleets and admirals. The book is patriotic instruction, openly and ably done.
19968-a-busy-year-at-the-old-squire-s:
C. A. Stephens wrote A Busy Year at the Old Squire's, dated 1922. Master Joel Pierson arrives on a Sunday afternoon as promised. His Thanksgiving Eve letter said he would come. He takes up his abode at the old Squire's for the winter school term. Stephens' Maine farm household gathers another young member. The busy year of the title gets its full cast early.

Stephens wrote the Old Squire series for The Youth's Companion. His farm tales ran for decades and taught rural skills by story. Winter term, chores, and schooling structure this volume. The Squire's household is a small working commonwealth. Stephens preserves Maine farm life before tractors and electricity. His readers grew up inside these books.
20326-six-little-bunkers-at-uncle-fred-s:
Laura Lee Hope published Six Little Bunkers at Uncle Fred's in 1918. Front matter lists her Outdoor Girls books for eager young readers. Titles run from Deepdale and Rainbow Lake to Florida and Pine Island. Such lists show how series books sold each other to loyal fans.

The Six Little Bunkers are siblings whose trips spark mild, funny mishaps. At Uncle Fred's, ranch or farm life gives them room to roam. Each book keeps danger low and family warmth high throughout. Young readers get cheerful adventures built for bedtime-length chapters.
20374-capitals-a-primer-of-information-a:
The Use of Capitals is a short primer on when English writers should use capital letters. It lays out rules in plain order and backs each rule with examples. Ben Franklin's saying that honesty is the best policy appears as one of the model quotations.

The rules cover quotations, names of God and the Trinity, the Virgin Mary, and the Devil. The book is careful to note when a word stays small, as when devil is only a general term or a swear word. Printers, clerks, and students of the time used such primers to keep their writing correct.
20377-the-23rd-service-battalion-royal-f:
During the First World War, the 23rd Service Battalion of the Royal Fusiliers was raised from sportsmen. Cricketers, hunters, and games players left green English fields to learn the soldier's trade. Their battalion became known as the First Sportsmen's Battalion.

Verses in the book catch the spirit of the men who joined. They came new to war, the poem says, but they did not care what game they played so long as they played the game. The record preserves how a battalion built from the sporting world faced the sweat and danger of the trenches.
20699-dotty-dimple-at-her-grandmother-s:
Sophie May's Dotty Dimple at Her Grandmother's belongs to the Dotty Dimple books, among the first American series written for very young children. Little Dotty goes on a visit to her grandmother's house. Her prattle, scrapes, and sudden generosities fill the short chapters.

The visit opens on a May morning. Everything was very fresh and beautiful, as if God had just made the world. The new grass had begun to grow, and the fields were dotted with short, golden-topped dandelions. Sophie May's gentle scenes taught generations of small readers their first chapter books.
22008-st-cuthbert-s:
Robert E. Knowles, a Canadian minister, published St. Cuthbert's in 1905. The book sold so fast that five editions appeared within months. Its narrator is a young Presbyterian minister taking charge of his first parish in Canada. The opening chapters show him parting from Tom, a friend who waits, like him, for a call to a church.

From the kirk session's first meetings, parish life supplies every kind of test. The minister visits homes, faces a secret in one man's past, and tries to win rough workmen without losing their employers. One bold proposal puts him between labour and capital. Knowles writes with humour and warmth about faith at work in a raw new town.
22053-stories-of-king-arthur-and-his-kni:
U. Waldo Cutler retold Thomas Malory's Morte d'Arthur as Stories of King Arthur and His Knights. Malory's great book, finished in prison in the 1400s, gathers the whole Arthur legend. Cutler kept the matter but smoothed the old language for younger readers. Knights, quests, and enchantments follow in steady order.

Chapters tell of Sir Galahad, Sir Lancelot, and Sir Tristram and the fair Isoud. Tristram drinks the love potion meant for King Mark, and sorrow follows. The Round Table's glory and its fall stand behind every tale. Retellings like Cutler's carried Malory into schoolrooms and homes that would never face the original's spelling.
22584-four-years-in-rebel-capitals-an-in:
Four Years in Rebel Capitals is a memoir of life in the Confederate South during the Civil War, issued by the Gossip Printing Company. The writer spent the war years inside the South's capitals and recorded how great events felt to the people living through them. No personal author is named in the catalog record.

In the preface, the writer is modest about the work's scope. The pages claim only to be simple notes on events and on how those events changed the mental and moral tone of southern people. That focus on mood over battle plans sets the book apart from standard campaign histories. It serves readers who want the home-front feel of the Confederacy from someone who watched it daily.
2297-snow-bound-at-eagle-s:
Bret Harte traps a party of travelers in a Sierra snowstorm in Snow-Bound at Eagle's, a novella of enforced intimacy. Strangers thrown together in a mountain station reveal secrets, romances, and old grudges as the snow piles up outside. Harte uses the storm as a stage for his favorite types: gamblers, schoolmarms, and reformed rogues.

The story's charm lies in its dialogue and its slow thaw of suspicion into affection. Winter danger sharpens every exchange. Readers will find a cozy yet tense California tale, perfect for a snowy evening.
23183-edmond-dante-s:
Edmond Dantès is an anonymous sequel to the famous novel of the Count of Monte Cristo. The publisher's notice in the text says the story picks up at once where the earlier book closed. It promises readers the same mix of delight, instruction, and strong feeling that made the first tale so popular.

The notice praises the sequel's cleverness, originality, and power to hold attention. Dantès, the wronged sailor who rose to wealth and revenge as the Count, remains at the centre of the tale. Readers who finished the first book curious about what came next are the clear audience for this continuation.
23267-the-cannibal-islands-captain-cook-:
The Cannibal Islands tells of Captain Cook's adventures in the South Seas. It opens by praising its hero in the highest terms. Cook's name, it says, is known wherever books are read, though he was born into the humblest station.

He climbed to the very top of fame, and he was self-taught in doing it. No large sums or long years were spent on his schooling, and no college made him what he was. Readers get a popular life of Cook written for admiration: a poor boy whose skill and courage carried him across the Pacific.
23504-the-story-of-nelson-also-the-grate:
W. H. G. Kingston gathered three short stories of roughly equal length in this small book, which has, oddly, no page numbers at all. The first tells of Nelson, as if written by an admirer whose sea work kept him near the great admiral.

The second turns to farming in the Red River country of North America in the late seventeen hundreds or early eighteen hundreds, where river floods and native neighbours made life hard. The third follows a lad of no more than fourteen who wins note in battle and gains a midshipman's rank at once. He rises through prizes and brave service to admiral and baronet, past jealous rivals. Kingston tells all three with warmth, making a pleasant trio of sea, settlement, and a boy's rise.
23635-wampum-a-paper-presented-to-the-nu:
Ashbel Woodward, a Connecticut physician, read this essay before the Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Philadelphia in January 1868, and it was printed at Albany in 1878. His subject is wampum: the strings of shell beads that Native peoples of the northeast made, wore, gave as welcome gifts, and used in trade and treaty.

Woodward begins with Columbus receiving shell beads on his second voyage. He goes on to trace how wampum was made, valued, and exchanged, and what it meant in dealings between Native nations and Europeans. For collectors and students of early America, it remains a clear early study of an object that was at once ornament, money, and record.
24772-sara-crewe-or-what-happened-at-mis:
Frances Hodgson Burnett published Sara Crewe in 1888, in a Scribner edition dated 1891, with drawings by Reginald B. Birch. Sara, a rich man's daughter, comes to Miss Minchin's dull London school, where her doll Emily and her stories make her a favorite. When her father dies and the money is gone, Miss Minchin turns her into a half-starved servant.

Sara keeps her pride through cold attics, stale bread, and hard chores, holding to kindness and make-believe. Burnett writes with warmth for a brave child who refuses to grow bitter. The tale later grew into A Little Princess, but this shorter form stands on its own as a classic school story.
24998-concerning-bully-hayes-from-the-st:
Louis Becke's portrait of 'Bully' Hayes, from 'The Strange Adventure of James Shervinton' and published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1902, recalls the halcyon days of the eighteen-sixties and seventies in the Pacific. Queensland schooners and Hawaiian labour vessels ran the blackbirding trade, with government agents, drunk nine days in ten, drawing bonuses from planters under the table. Becke notes the Tahiti, lost with four hundred islanders aboard on their way to forced labour in San José de Guatemala.

Captain William Henry Hayes of Cleveland, Ohio, came twice a year to Samoa with oil, copra, and island labourers obtained on his peculiar time-payment system. German skippers fled his white-painted brig with Cunningham's patent topsails, for Hayes and his companion Ben Peese boarded Dutchmen and walked off with their chronometers. In Sydney and Melbourne he spent royally as a gay, dashing, black-whiskered Yankee captain.
25063-the-beggar-s-opera-to-which-is-pre:
John Gay's Beggar's Opera, in the 1921 Heinemann edition, is the great ballad opera of eighteenth-century London, here printed with the music to each song. The text follows the 1765 edition, with scenes renumbered in modern fashion and plates by Claud Lovat Fraser.

Gay sets thieves, highwaymen, and jailers to familiar tunes and turns them into a satire of politics, greed, and polite society. Polly Peachum, Captain Macheath, and Lucy Lockit scheme, sing, and betray one another in a Newgate underworld that mirrors the respectable world outside it. The opera's songs and wit made it a lasting stage favorite.
25221-philippian-studies-lessons-in-fait: H. C. G. Moule's Philippian Studies, in a third edition from Hodder and Stoughton in 1900, is known here only from its front matter and contents. The text supplied holds the title page, the author's preface from Ridley Hall, Cambridge, and chapter headings, with no lesson text. Its contents promise studies in faith and love from Paul's Epistle to the Philippians, opening with the intimacy of human hearts in Christ and the apostle's position and circumstances.
27495-the-girls-of-st-olave-s:
Mabel Mackintosh, author of The Doings of Denys, published this story of girls with John F. Shaw in London. Its chapters run from As Good as Gone and Love and Money through A Wild-Goose Chase, A Ticket for One, and Bearding the Lion, to The Hiding-Place and The Sun Shines Out.

The story opens with Gertrude telling Denys, positively, that engaged girls are no use to their families. All they think about, Gertrude says, is the postman and their bottom drawer. Denys answers with a good-tempered laugh. From that family comedy, the tale moves through shame, fear, tricks, and raids. Young readers get a lively school-age story.
27767-slavery-what-it-was-what-it-has-do:
Cydnor B. Tompkins of Ohio delivered this speech in the House of Representatives on April 24, 1860, on slavery: what it was, what it had done, and what it intended to do. He spoke as a Republican answering pro-slavery members.

Tompkins charges that the slavery party forced the subject on Congress and filled debate with threats and slander, while Republicans were blamed for the excitement. The speech is a sharp pre-Civil War statement of the Republican case against slavery's political power. Tompkins spoke after two months of debate carried on almost entirely by the slavery party.
2859-a-little-dinner-at-timmins-s:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote A Little Dinner at Timmins's as a comedy about a small household attempting a grand occasion. Fitzroy Timmins and his wife live in Lilliput Street, a genteel neighborhood near the park, and count themselves distantly related to the Earl of Bungay. Timmins keeps chambers in the Temple and rides the Northern Circuit as a barrister.

The dinner itself becomes a trial of menus, cooks, and guests, with a French chef named Cavalcadour producing pink and blue bills of fare from his pocketbook. Mrs. Timmins puzzles over the documents while social ambition outruns the household budget. Thackeray's satire stays affectionate, mocking a young couple who want to shine just a little beyond their means.
2897-the-sequel-of-appomattox-a-chronicl:
Walter Lynwood Fleming wrote The Sequel of Appomattox, volume thirty-two of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. The book traces reunion after the Civil War through chapters on the aftermath of war and the work of the presidents. Later chapters cover the wards of the nation, the victory of the radicals, and the trial of President Johnson. Fleming treats Reconstruction as a political struggle rather than a settled story.

The narrative quotes generals reporting from the South, including complaints about agents who demanded special privileges for freed people while excusing lawlessness. Such passages show the period's arguments in their own terms. The book gives readers a compact account of reunion, written a half century after Appomattox and before later revision changed the field.
29098-black-bass-where-to-catch-them-in-:
W. P. Pond and Company published this fishing guide in New York in 1888. Its promise is plain in the title: black bass in quantity, within an hour's ride of New York City. The book treats the best methods and baits in full, with practical hints on rods and tackle.

It also reviews weather signs and atmospheric influences, so an angler can read the sky before heading out. A short verse on the fly-fisher's quiet life sets the tone. Readers get a compact Victorian sporting manual, useful as history of New York fishing waters and as a still-readable guide to bass habits and tackle.
30293-the-candy-maker-s-guide-a-collecti:
The Fletcher Manufacturing Company of Toronto compiles and publishes The Candy Maker's Guide, a collection of choice recipes for sugar boiling, printed by John Johnston in Toronto in 1896. Fletcher, makers of confectioners' and candy makers' tools and machines, tea and coffee urns, and bakers', confectioners', and hotel supplies, also imported and dealt in pure fruit juices. Flavoring extracts, fruit oils, essential oils, malt extract, and XXXX glucose followed.

A prize medal and diploma awarded at the Toronto Industrial Exhibition of 1894 fronts the volume from 440 to 442 Yonge Street. It cites general excellence in style and finish of goods. Fletcher also made and dealt in generators, steel and copper soda water cylinders, soda founts, tumbler washers, freezers, and ice breaking machines. Ice cream refrigerators, milk shakers, ice shaves, lemon squeezers, ice cream cans, and packing tubs followed, with golden and crystal flake for ice cream.
30895-rembrandt-and-his-etchings-a-compa:
Louis A. Holman wrote this compact record of Rembrandt's life, work, and time, published by Charles E. Goodspeed and Company in Boston in 1921, with a complete chronological list of his etchings compiled by A. M. Hind of the British Museum. Its plates include Rembrandt leaning on a stone sill, Two Tramps, Rembrandt's Mother, Omval, Jan Lutma the goldsmith and sculptor, and Jacob and Laban.

Holman opens in Leyden, described through the fresh eager eyes of the youthful William Bradford when the English exiles sought asylum in Holland. Rembrandt, he notes, had just been born there when the pilgrims came to the university town. The book pairs a short life with a full etching list, for readers who want Rembrandt's art in order, plate by plate.
30897-a-little-housekeeping-book-for-a-l:
Caroline French Benton wrote this little housekeeping book for a little girl, subtitled Margaret's Saturday Mornings, published by the Page Company in Boston as part of the Ideal Series for Girls. Its premise, stated on the title page, is simple: a little girl, home from school on Saturday mornings, finds out how to make helpful use of her spare time. Margaret is the girl at the center of the lessons.

Twelve chapters move from Margaret's Christmas tree and the kitchen fire through the dining-room table, washing dishes, care of the bedrooms, sweeping and dusting, and the bathroom, brasses, and grates. They end with housecleaning, laundry work, the linen closet, marketing and keeping accounts, and the day's work. It is a gentle, practical manual of early twentieth-century housekeeping for young readers.
30956-history-of-the-great-american-fort:
Gustavus Myers wrote this first volume of his History of the Great American Fortunes, published by Charles H. Kerr in Chicago in 1910, with copyrights from 1907 to 1909. Myers had already written histories of Tammany Hall and of public franchises in New York City. Volume one has two parts: conditions in settlement and colonial times, and the great land fortunes.

Part one treats great proprietary estates, the sway of the landgraves, the rise of the trading class, and shipping fortunes, with Stephen Girard as the richest of the shippers. Part two traces the origin of huge city estates and the Astor fortune through its inception, growth, ramifications, momentum, propulsion, and climax, with other land fortunes and the Field fortune in full. Myers writes a critical, muckraking history of how great wealth was made in America.
31157-hymns-from-the-greek-office-books-:
The Reverend John Brownlie's 1904 volume, printed at Paisley by Alexander Gardner, renders hymns from the Greek office books into English. It adds centos, or patchwork hymns stitched from older lines, and suggestions for use. Brownlie, already known for his hymns of the Greek and Eastern churches, gives both a Greek index and English texts for worship.

The hymns follow the church year and its feasts, from the cross and the tomb to the ascension, with prayers for mercy, light, and the Spirit woven through. For singers and scholars, the book opens the rich chant tradition of the Eastern church to English readers who could not follow the Greek originals.
31312-air-service-boys-over-the-enemy-s-:
Charles Amory Beach's 1919 boys' book, published by the World Syndicate Publishing Company, follows Tom and Jack, American aviators fighting for France. It opens with a puzzle: a man looking like a French peasant, yet not one, discovered near the aviation camp hangars, who vanishes like smoke once the hue and cry is raised. That raises the question whether he is a German spy.

Twenty-five chapters carry the chums over the enemy's lines, through a moonlight flight, a landing close to Metz, a lone house by the roadside, and a nest of spies. They also visit an old Lorraine château, with Jack left behind in enemy country before a return to safety. Brisk and patriotic, the book is wartime aviation adventure for boy readers.
31316-the-coming-of-evolution-the-story-:
John W. Judd's 1910 volume in the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature, printed at the University Press, tells how evolution came to science. Twelve chapters trace the idea from its origins and its extension to the inorganic world, through the triumph of catastrophism and the revolt of Scrope and Lyell. They also trace Lyell's Principles of Geology and its influence.

Later chapters take up early attempts at an organic doctrine, Darwin and Wallace with natural selection, The Origin of Species, and the influence of Darwin's works. They also cover the place of Lyell and Darwin in history, with portraits of Darwin, Scrope, Lyell, and Wallace. Clear and compact, the book remains a fine short history of a great revolution.
31352-sex-education-a-series-of-lectures:
Maurice A. Bigelow, professor of biology at Teachers College, Columbia University, wrote Sex-Education, a series of lectures concerning knowledge of sex in its relation to human life, published by the Macmillan Company in 1916. Dedicated to the memory of Dr. Prince A. Morrow, the book argues from Bigelow's trust in human nature's basic goodness, as the dedication puts it. Its lectures treat sex as a subject for honest, scientific teaching rather than silence.

Bigelow addresses teachers, parents, and students, setting out what young people should be told and how it should be taught. The lectures belong to the early sex-education movement, which sought to replace ignorance with biology and ethics. Modern readers will find both the science of its day and the moral framework of its time, and a clear record of how reformers argued for frank instruction.
31646-through-our-unknown-southwest-the-:
Agnes C. Laut's Through Our Unknown Southwest, the wonderland of the United States, little known and unappreciated, was published at New York by McBride, Nast, and Company in May 1913. It saw a second printing in October. Laut was already the author of The Conquest of the Great Northwest, Lords of the North, and Freebooters of the Wilderness. Her frontispiece shows Montezuma's Castle, the ruined cliff dwelling on Beaver Creek in Arizona.

The book is the home of the cliff dweller and the Hopi, the forest ranger and the Navajo, and it follows the lure of the Painted Desert. Laut's travel book opens a little-known country to readers, with its ruins, its peoples, and its desert light.
32693-that-boy-of-norcott-s:
Charles James Lever tells of a boy torn between parents who have ceased to live together. A Dublin trial over his guardianship opens the tale: the child, then seven, was to live alternate years with each parent, a plan his mother's friends warned would wreck his character.

His father, Captain Sir Roger Norcott of the Dragoons, met his mother, a watchmaker's gentle daughter of eighteen, while quartered at Macroom in Ireland. The boy grows up between luxury and longing, fearing his father's eye and voice, and yearning for a pittance and a life of his own.
32967-a-sketch-book-of-r-caldecott-s:
A Sketch-Book of R. Caldecott's, reproduced by Edmund Evans the engraver and printer and published by George Routledge and Sons, gathers the artist's drawings across the seasons and subjects he loved. Its pages run from intense students of nature and the seasons, green peas and March and spring, to Siena, San Gimignano, and a review of the household troops, cavalry, infantry, and spectators. Verses on spring and love sit beside the pictures.

Caldecott's charm lies in quick, lively line and in humor that never turns cruel, and Evans's reproduction keeps the drawings fresh. The book is less a formal biography than a portfolio, letting readers leaf through an artist's eye at work. For lovers of Victorian illustration and children's picture books, it is a delightful volume to browse, full of movement, weather, and good temper.
33239-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers entries from Cat to Celt, in alphabetical order. Its articles range over places, peoples, history, science, and art, each written by a specialist and set out in the dense, exact style of the great reference work. Readers will find long treatments of major topics beside short entries on smaller terms, all cross-linked by the alphabet itself.

As a slice of the famous eleventh edition, the volume shows how knowledge was summed up before the First World War: thorough, confident, and rich in detail. It serves best as a work to dip into, whether for a place name, a tribe, a thinker, or a term in science. Scholars still prize this edition for its depth, and this volume gives a full taste of its scope and method.
34115-our-battalion-being-some-slight-im:
L. Raven-Hill's 1902 book Our Battalion offers light sketches of His Majesty's Auxiliary Forces in camp and elsewhere. Issued from the Punch office in London, it treats volunteers with the same comic eye that marked the magazine.

Short pieces take up recruits, drill, the system, the general in command, the seven ages of the volunteer, a lost patrol, and camp diaries kept by officers. The humour is gentle and the drawings do much of the work, making the book a fond record of part-time soldiering at play and drill. Two camp diaries, kept in the voices of a lieutenant-colonel and a captain-adjutant, close the comic round.
34190-h-m-s:
Klaxon wrote this book of naval sketches and stories, published in Edinburgh and London in 1918 by William Blackwood and Sons, dedicated to D. V. B. Contents run from 1923 and Privileged through According to Their Lights and a naval discussion. The gunlayer, a wage slave, an annual, mascots, the sparrow, and a war wedding follow.

Later pieces cover a hymn of disgust, the special, between tides, and light cavalry. A trinity, in the morning, an affair of outposts, 1917, in forty west, chances, the quartermaster, a landfall, night rounds, and the barred zone follow. Klaxon writes of wartime navy life with humor. The book offers a sailor's view of the Great War at sea.
34201-an-amicable-controversy-with-a-jew:
Park wrote An Amicable Controversy with a Jewish Rabbi on the Messiah's Coming, published at London in 1832 by Smith, Elder. The catalog gives his name as Park, a physician. The book unfolds new views on prophecy and the nature of the millennium, with an entirely new exposition of the prophet Zechariah.

The contents work through Zechariah chapter by chapter: Park's interpretation, notes on the Hebrew punctuation, then the rabbi's exposition and reply, then Park's remarks on the reply. The exchange stays amicable, as the title promises, which was not the custom of such books. Both men argue from the same Hebrew text toward opposite hopes. The volume is a specimen of the prophecy literature that filled the eighteen thirties. Respect and conviction share its pages.
34256-the-supply-at-saint-agatha-s:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps wrote The Supply at Saint Agatha's, published by Houghton, Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1896. E Boyd Smith and Marcia Oakes Woodbury drew the illustrations. Saint Agatha's stands at the crossing of an old avenue with the stream of present traffic. The city is not named. The church is eminent, with a stately date on its foundation stone. Its pew-list stands unsurpassed among the worshipers of the Eastern States.

Saint Agatha's is known for three things: its money, its music, and its soundness. Its wardens stand high on the town tax-list, read slowly by mechanics and strikers on Saturday nights. Its choir alone would fill the house; its soprano is a famous prima donna. In church position it has always stood above reproach. When did Saint Agatha's question a canon, Phelps asks.
34347-dave-porter-in-the-south-seas-or-t:
Dave Porter in the South Seas is a boys' adventure novel from Edward Stratemeyer's Dave Porter series. The publisher's front matter lists Stratemeyer's many series, from the Old Glory war books to the Colonial and Pan-American tales. Dave Porter at Oak Hall precedes this volume in its own series.

The subtitle promises the strange cruise of the Stormy Petrel. Dave's school friends and rivals sail with him into the Pacific. The series list at the front shows the factory scale of Stratemeyer production. Scores of volumes, all cloth bound and illustrated, sold at set prices to boy readers. Adventure followed a reliable pattern of travel, danger, and manly pluck. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
34568-johann-sebastian-bach-the-story-of:
Johann Sebastian Bach, The Story of the Boy Who Sang in the Streets, is a child's life of Bach. Thomas Tapper wrote it for a Child's Own Book of Great Musicians series. The Presser company published it at Philadelphia with rights dated nineteen fifteen. Pictures on nearly every page show the places and people of the tale.

Sebastian was born at Eisenach in Germany, where his birth house still stands. The Wartburg castle on its hill watched over his boyhood games and climbs. His father Ambrosius was a musician, as Bachs had been for generations. A miller ancestor played and sang while his corn ground in the mill. Orphaned at ten, Sebastian went to live with an elder brother nearby. By moonlight he copied out music his brother had forbidden him to play.
35050-organizing-and-building-up-the-sun:
Organizing and Building Up the Sunday School is a guide book by Jesse Lyman Hurlbut, out in nineteen ten. It is one of a set of such guides for the new church school, shaped by two named hands. Parts treat the past rules of that move, the laws of the school, and the need of ranks by age. The chief, his aids, the writ hand, and the purse each take parts.

The school book store and its run take two parts, and the drills of the teach hand take two more. The folk the school may draw and the ways to draw them close the main text. Hurlbut meant the book as a hand book for the plain reader. Past a call to serve as a class book too, he set black board lines and test asks at the back, past a change of the main text.
35305-mr-punch-s-pocket-ibsen-a-collecti:
Mr Punch Pocket Ibsen is a jest set of short Ibsen plays by Anstey. Bernard Partridge drew the cuts for the book, out in eighteen ninety three. Its full name calls the plays shrunk, fixed, and slid for keen school folk. The plays first ran in the pages of Punch sheet in their day. Rosmersholm, Nora, Hedda Gabler, and The Wild Duck fill the scheme.

A fifth piece, Pill Doctor Herdal, is Anstey own stab at the mold. He grants it lacks the deep fog and mad folk of the true Ibsen. Nora bears the next name of the bird cage in his scheme jest. Rebecca West knits a vast mat as the first play opens in a fine room. Madam Helseth lays the meal board while white horse talk starts the fun.
36251-the-corner-house-girls-on-a-tour-w:
The Corner House Girls on a Tour, by Grace Brooks Hill, bears a copyright of 1917. Hill had written two earlier books about the same girls. The tale opens on a Saturday morning in the big kitchen of the old Corner House at Milton.

The four Kenway girls chatter like sparrows while the house staff is still abed. Soon a big tour is planned, and the party takes to the road in an automobile. Chapters bring a wayside camp, a six-foot rattler, and time spent with Romany folk. Sammy, the boy of the house, plays sleuth more than once. A green and orange petticoat serves as a clue, and the tin badge of the law turns up late in the tale.
36322-the-battleship-boys-at-sea-or-two-:
The Battleship Boys at Sea, by Frank Gee Patchin, follows two lads who join the United States Navy. Patchin wrote other books in the same series, and this one is billed as the tale of two apprentices in Uncle Sam's Navy. It opens in a town street, where Dan Davis spots a sign across the road.

Dan asks a policeman the way to the Navy recruiting station, and Sam Hickey goes with him. The pair gaze at a poster of a sailor and a white battleship under palm trees. The parts ahead promise hammocks, the rifle range, a first detail, and work on a mine field. One part is called Buried Three Fathoms Deep, and the last is named Heroes to the Rescue.
36340-from-chart-house-to-bush-hut-being:
Bryde wrote From Chart House to Bush Hut, the record of a sailor's seven years in the Queensland bush. The chart house is the small room on a ship where the charts live and the course is laid. The bush hut is its far opposite, a rough shelter in the Australian wilds. Bryde traded one for the other and wrote the change down.

Seven years of clearing, fencing, mustering, and battling drought and flood make his record. Sailors often took to the bush in the old days, and few told the tale so fully. Snakes, storms, and loneliness share the pages with mateship and humor. Readers get two hard lives in one book, salt water first and then red dust.
36395-ruth-fielding-in-the-red-cross-or-:
Alice Emerson's Ruth Fielding in the Red Cross, or Doing Her Best for Uncle Sam, was published by Cupples and Leon of New York in 1918. The series list at the front prices the Ruth Fielding books at fifty cents a volume, postpaid, with a dozen earlier volumes behind this one. This volume and Ruth Fielding at the War Front carry her into the war.

Twenty-five chapters follow Ruth's war work: Uncle Jabez excited, the call of the drum, the boys of the draft, the patriotism of the purse. Then she sails through dangerous waters to a change of base, the gateway of the chateau, and the wayside cross. Chapter one opens on her packing a box for the local Red Cross chapter, when news comes that stops her, horrified, mid-task: not Tom, she cries, looking up at the speaker.
3663-the-girl-from-keller-s:
Harold Bindloss writes a western Canadian novel about Festing, a farmer on the Saskatchewan prairie. The book, published in England as Sadie's Conquest, opens at dusk as Festing stops at the edge of a ravine, having walked fast from his work through leafless birches. The wide landscape lies desolate in fading light, but Festing knows a change is coming that will end its silence.

The girl from Keller's is Sadie, whose arrival tests Festing's plans and his heart. Bindloss writes prairie farming, trails, and homestead life with practical detail. The novel suits readers who enjoy Canadian frontier romance, where land, weather, and hard work shape a love story.
37104-the-demands-of-rome-her-own-story-:
Elizabeth Schoffen wrote The Demands of Rome, her own story of thirty-one years as a Sister of Charity in the Roman Catholic Church, under the name Sister Lucretia. She published the second edition herself at Portland, Oregon, in 1917. Portraits show her in her sister's dress and as a lecturer. She dedicates the book to two American friends and benefactors, and says many entreaties led her to tell her story at last.

Schoffen writes against the church she served, in the manner of the ex-nun narratives that were common in the period. Readers should weigh her account as one side of a bitter argument. It documents a popular anti-Catholic literature of its day.
37147-the-cricket-s-friends-tales-told-b:
The Cricket's Friends holds tales told by the Cricket, the Teapot, and the Saucepan, written by Cousin Virginia for children. Worthington printed the book in New York in 1888, though the text was first entered in 1868. It continues an earlier volume about a club of kitchen things.

The club meets around the hearth, where small creatures and pots talk. The Cricket brings in new members: a traveled spider, a disappointed caterpillar, and an ambitious wasp. The Teapot doubts the strangers, and the Cricket scolds her for poor manners. The tales that follow include silver peaches, a grandpapa mouse, and an enchanted baby house. Cousin Virginia writes gentle wonder for young listeners at story time.
37359-motor-truck-logging-methods-engine:
Motor Truck Logging Methods is an engineering experiment station bulletin on hauling logs by motor truck. The study treats trucks as a working system, not a novelty. Its chapters cover loading and unloading logs. A section on tires follows the running gear through the work. Tables carry the costs of operation.

Cost accounts run through the bulletin in detail. Depreciation is reckoned on a four-year basis for the trucks. Tables spread the figures across the working day, morning and afternoon. The bulletin belongs to the years when motor trucks were displacing horses and rail spurs in the woods. Logging engineers needed hard numbers: what a truck cost per day, how loads were handled, and where time went. The station's tables answer with records rather than opinion. For operators weighing a fleet, the comparison of methods was the point of the study.
37625-our-old-home-vol-2-annotated-with-:
Our Old Home, volume two, is Nathaniel Hawthorne's book of English sketches, in an annotated edition from Houghton, Mifflin. The Riverside Press printed it in 1891, with notes drawn from Hawthorne's own notebook and pictures in photogravure. The first copyright stands in 1863, Hawthorne's own. A portrait of Lord Nelson fronts the volume.

The pictures promise the matter: Blenheim, the Thames at Oxford, and Magdalen College from the Cherwell. The haunts of Burns follow, with his birthplace, the Auld Brig o' Doon, and Alloway Kirk. London views close the list: a suburb, the Houses of Parliament, the Tower, and Poets' Corner. The first sketch here, Near Oxford, sets out on a fine September morning for Blenheim in a four-horse carriage.
38265-my-life-in-many-states-and-in-fore:
My Life in Many States and in Foreign Lands, dictated in his seventy fourth year by George Francis Train, was printed in New York by D Appleton and Company in November 1902. A photo portrait of Train stands at the front. Train gives the book to the children and the children children in this and all lands who love and believe in him.

The first chapter treats when he was four years old, in 1833, with New Orleans then his home. Later chapters treat a shipping house in Boston from 1844 to 1850, where he rose fast. He sold Emerson a ticket for Liverpool and engaged Rufus Choate and Daniel Webster as the firm lawyers. His first speculation follows. Train was a famed merchant and speaker. Life fans get a brag life in the man own brisk voice.
38827-journeys-in-persia-and-kurdistan-v:
Journeys in Persia and Kurdistan, Volume 1, is a travel narrative by Mrs Bishop, Isabella L Bird, published by John Murray of London in 1891. The work runs to two volumes and is written as letters. This volume takes in a summer in the Upper Karun region and a visit to the Nestorian rayahs.

A portrait of the author fronts the book, with maps and illustrations after. Plates show a Turkish frontier fort and Persian bread-making. The shrine of Fatima, a dervish, and the castle of Ardal appear. The Karun at Dupulan and a Bakhtiari cradle close the list. A glossary explains Persian terms for the untravelled many, to whom the volumes are dedicated. Bird was already famed for Unbeaten Tracks in Japan. The letters record lodgings, escorts, bread, and shrines with a traveller's exact eye.
38828-journeys-in-persia-and-kurdistan-v:
Isabella Bird, as Mrs Bishop, told of roads in Persia and Kurdistan. Volume two of two is this copy of her road set. The book came out in London in 1891 with maps and plates. A front plate shows the church of Mar Shalita at Kochanes. She wrote Six Months in the Sandwich Islands in past years.

A summer in the Upper Karun lands fills part of this book. A call on the Nestorian Rayahs stands in its sub-title as well. Towns, hills, and church folk of old rite fill her road tale. Her eye miss naught on those hard, wild roads she rode. Bird's fame as a bold guest of far lands crowns the work. Road fans get a queen's tale.
38896-the-hollow-tree-snowed-in-book-bei:
The Hollow Tree Snowed In Book continues the stories of the Hollow Tree and Deep Woods people, by Albert Bigelow Paine, issued in 1910. Pictures show the whole company at the front: Mister Crow, Turtle, Coon, Possum, Robin, Squirrel, Dog, and Rabbit. Paine had written the first Hollow Tree book before, and his other works are listed with their prices.

In this volume the deep woods folk are snowed in together for the winter. One picture caption has Mister Dog telling how he knows all about menageries, for he has been to one. Tales told round the fire while the snow holds them in are the frame of the book. Paine wrote these animal stories for children in a plain, droll voice that adults of his day also read with pleasure.
39274-baron-bruno-or-the-unbelieving-phi:
Baron Bruno, or The Unbelieving Philosopher, and Other Fairy Stories was written by Louisa Morgan and published in London in 1875. Caldecott drew the pictures, including a frontispiece called Esgair. Five tales fill the small book for young readers.

Baron Bruno, prime minister to a grand duke, is the cleverest man in his kingdom. His lack of belief drives the title tale, with the stars playing their part. Esgair, the bride of Llyn Idwyl, turns to Welsh legend for its matter. Eothwald the young sculptor and Fido and Fidunia follow in turn. A last tale tells of Eudaemon, an enchanter of the north. Readers get Victorian fairy tales with a moral bent and fine drawings.
40840-ten-years-among-the-mail-bags-or-n:
Ten Years Among the Mail Bags holds tales of mail crime by J Holbrook. The author served as a special agent of the post office arm. Prints dress the diary tales of theft hunts in the mails. The book came out in the year eighteen fifty five.

The front note says all folk crave the tale of how mail thieves are caught. It hopes the tales will make the mails safe and school the staff. Tricks of theft, marks on bags, and traps for the staff fill the parts. Each tale names the mode of the crime and the snare that won. The gift page sends the book to all who serve the mails.
4125-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1660:
The complete diary for 1660 carries Samuel Pepys through the year that made him, from a clerk in a shifting state to a Navy Office man under a restored king. Entries move between office, Whitehall, church, and home, with money, clothes, and dinners noted beside affairs of state.

Editorial notes in this edition catch even Pepys's own slips, such as his blunder over his wedding date, and show how the diary was kept and read. The year's arc runs from winter uncertainty to the king's return and a new life. Readers who want Pepys whole should start here, where the great diary finds its stride.
41300-daniel-webster-for-young-americans:
A school edition of Daniel Webster's speeches, published at Boston in 1907. Little, Brown and Company issued the volume. Charles F Richardson of Dartmouth College supplied the notes. Portraits and historical scenes illustrate the text richly. Webster's birthplace and Dartmouth career open a chronology. He was born in New Hampshire in January 1782.

The speeches chosen are the patriotic monuments. Plymouth's first settlement and Bunker Hill's monument lead. Adams and Jefferson's eulogy follows in full. The Reply to Hayne anchors the collection at greatest length. The character of Washington and the Constitution and the Union close it. A murder trial argument shows Webster the lawyer. Generations of schoolboys learned oratory from these pages. Webster's face, from a daguerreotype, fronts the book.
4131-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1661:
The complete diary for 1661 follows Pepys through a year of growing office income and standing. On January 1, Mr. Moore brings his last month's papers to sign and tells him, to his great comfort, that his fees will come to eighty pounds clear, with more from pardons.

Through the year Pepys works at the Navy Office, dines with captains and clerks, and watches his household grow. The full-year form lets readers trace money, marriage, and career across seasons without a break. It suits anyone who wants Pepys's second great year in one continuous run.
41326-the-girls-of-st-wode-s:
The Girls of St Wode's, by Meade, was published at New York. Grosset and Dunlap issued the school story. Meade had written Deb and the Duchess before. Thirty three chapters make the book. Preparing for the young debutantes opens it. A third class carriage and a torn dress follow. The girls' bedrooms and the modern view of life come early. St Wode's College itself is reached at chapter eleven. Inky Annie, cocoa parties, and freshers fill the school part. A guild, a picnic, and twins lighten the middle. Handwriting, a missing key, and a confession close the list. Chapter one brings three sisters home from school.

Eileen, Marjorie, and Letitia Chetwynd are expected on an April day. Their mother, a fashionable widow, returned from India two years before. Her friend Acheson, plainer and poorer, shares the drawing room talk.
4138-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1662:
The complete diary for 1662 opens with a comic mishap. Waking suddenly, Pepys hits his wife a great blow over face and nose with his elbow, waking her in pain, to his sorrow. Up, he goes forth with Sir William Pen by coach toward Westminster, passing Spanish sights along the way.

Through the year, Portsmouth journeys, Deptford payings, and court meetings build a portrait of a Navy man rising. The full-year run lets readers follow money, marriage, and office across seasons. It suits those who want Pepys's 1662 without a break, from elbow mishaps to yard business.
4145-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1663:
The complete diary for 1663 gathers Pepys's full year, from winter lodgings at his lord's house to autumn councils on seamen's riots. He walks Whitehall with growing confidence, settles the Brampton estate with his father, and works the Navy Office through its seasons.

Money, marriage, and office favor thread the year, with dinners, music, and church beside them. Reading the year whole shows how a clerk's daily notes add up to a portrait of Restoration England. The volume suits readers ready for Pepys at full stretch, in one unbroken run. No month is skipped, and no mood is smoothed away.
4153-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1664:
The complete diary for 1664 opens after midnight, Pepys going to bed between four and five with his mind in good temper. Sleeping till eight, he wakes to callers, among them a bearer of the best New Year's gift he ever had: a bill of exchange from Mr. Deering.

Through the year, office work, stone worries, and rising wealth share the page with dinners and music. Reading 1664 whole shows a man counting his fortune while his body warns him. The volume suits readers who want a full Pepys year, from New Year's gifts to winter accounts.
41616-reminiscences-of-a-private-by-fran:
Reminiscences of a Private is a war memoir by Frank Mixson. The author served in Company E of the first South Carolina corps. His unit marched in a brigade of Lees army in the war of the states. The book came out in the year nineteen ten.

A front print shows the old man forty five years past his war days. The gift page sends the book to sons and girls of the lost cause. It bids them pass the tale of grit, pain, and want to their own kin. Camp, march, and field tales fill the rank and file view of the war. The book stands as a foot mans own voice from the south side.
4162-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1665:
The complete diary for 1665 opens on a Lord's day, Pepys long in bed after a busy late night, then up to order accounts and papers for last year's gains and expense. He finds them very great, and sets about dividing the new year's business.

From that accounting start, the year runs into plague, as Tangier payments, ducal audiences, and river journeys give way to sickness and flight. Reading 1665 whole shows a rising man meeting a dying city. The volume stands beside 1666 as the diary's twin peak of history and daily life.
4171-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1666:
The complete diary for 1666 opens on New Year's Day with Pepys dictating pursers' business to Tooker from five in the morning, without food till three, then dining with Gibson in content. From that hard start the year runs through war, plague's tail, and the Great Fire.

Pepys's worth climbs past fifty-seven hundred pounds in August, then fire takes the city he served. Reading the year whole gives the fire its full weight, as months of work burn in days. The volume stands as the diary's most famous year, and its most terrible.
4184-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1667:
The complete diary for 1667 opens on a bitter, cold, frosty day, the frost grown old and the Thames covered with ice. Pepys works at the office all morning, then walks the Change with Houblon, speaking of their ill condition in money matters.

From frozen January the year runs through the Dutch raid, the Chatham disgrace, and the inquiries that followed. Reading 1667 whole shows a Navy man facing his service's worst summer and answering for it. The volume stands as the diary's year of reckoning, cold at both ends. From frozen river to Dutch raid, the year never lets up.
4195-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1668:
The complete diary for 1668 opens with Pepys making up accounts in his chamber against the new year, then going abroad with his wife to a dinner at Mrs. Pierce's that he has no mind to join. He finds his wife troubled at his ways, and the year unfolds from that domestic strain.

Through 1668, office work, theater, and parliamentary inquiries share the page, with the diary nearing its end. Reading the year whole shows a man winding down a great record without losing its frankness. The volume suits readers following Pepys toward his final entries.
4199-diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1669:
The complete diary for 1669 opens on New Year's Day with a noble silver warming pan presented by Captain Beckford, which Pepys doubts whether to take or not. With Hewer he goes to the New Exchange, then to cabinet shops to agree on a cabinet as a New Year's gift for his wife.

The year is the diary's last, short and poignant, ending where Pepys's eyesight and career turn him from daily writing. Reading 1669 whole gives the great record its quiet close, with gifts, cabinets, and farewells. The volume suits readers who want to see how Pepys laid down his pen.
41997-the-light-keepers-a-story-of-the-u:
The Light Keepers is a tale of the United States light house corps by James Otis. A Dutton house of New York brought it out in print of nineteen oh six. Sammy Peters, first aide at Carys Ledge light, spots a boat from the lamp glass. His face bears a war scar from a Petersburg shot of the civil war. Captain Eph Downs, his old war mate, leads the light post there.

Parts run through a lad named Sidney Harlow and plans for days to come. A motor boat fix, a close shave, and a sea trip fill the mid parts. Wreck and save work stand at the heart of the tale scheme. Storm bound days, an inspector call, and a form from the grave close it. Plates show famed lights from Cape Elizabeth to Matinicus in the scheme.
42317-industrial-arts-design-a-textbook-:
Industrial Arts Design is a textbook by William H Varnum of the University of Wisconsin, published in nineteen sixteen. It belongs to a vocational education series and is aimed at students, teachers, and craftsmen. A photograph of a kiln firing at the Rookwood Potteries fronts the book. Chapters break design down into mass and proportion.

The first chapters treat the primary mass of an object and its horizontal and vertical divisions. Appendages and details follow from those large choices. Pottery, furniture, and other craft forms give the working cases. The book teaches design as a set of steps that can be practised, not as taste alone. School manual arts courses were its market.
42650-the-boy-craftsman-practical-and-pr:
Neely Hall wrote a craft book full of work plans for a boy's free hours. More than four score times five plates aid the book. Hall and Norman Hall drew those plates by hand. The book's list names his craft books for boys and girls. A boy's own shop shows in a front plate in full gear.

Desks, toys, games, and camp gear fill the plans in turn. Each plan gives wood, tools, steps, and a drawn guide. Gain as well as fun is the book's boast in its title. A boy can make goods to use, to give, or to sell. Hall's clear voice made him a chief in boys' craft books. Home shops get a rich store.
43232-the-preparation-of-illustrations-f:
The Preparation of Illustrations for Reports of the United States Geological Survey is an official manual by John Ridgway, printed at Washington in 1920. It tells survey authors how to prepare pictures for reproduction in the Survey's published reports, and it appeared under the Department of the Interior, with George Otis Smith directing the Survey.

A first part covers preparation by authors: the purpose and value of illustrations, selection and approval, sizes, subdivisions of plates, and the preparation of maps from base material at standard scales. A second part describes the processes of reproduction themselves. Closing sections treat drawings of rock and fossil specimens, brush, pencil, and pen work, retouching photographs, landscape drawings from poor photographs, and drawings of crystals.
43464-lay-help-the-church-s-present-need:
William Baird, vicar of Homerton, read Lay Help, the Church's Present Need at St Mary's Schools, West Brompton, on November 17, 1870. Bartlett printed the paper in London that year, at the wish of Lord Lawrence and others who heard it. Baird owns the piece is rough and in parts, since he wrote it with no thought of print.

Baird holds that all church folk, of each party, feel one great want: lay help, well called out and well ruled. The first church, he notes, was a whole body of workers. Love for Christ showed in care for the poor and the sick. He urges set plans to draw out such help in each parish. The paper is a plain, warm plea for shared work in church life.
44853-letters-from-an-old-railway-offici:
Charles Delano Hine wrote a set of letters on rail work, printed in Chicago in nineteen hundred and four. The letters speak to his son, who has just become a division chief on a road. Hine says the son chose to work away from him so no one could claim he rose by help. A short piece by Frank H. Spearman comes at the end.

Each letter takes up one part of the job in plain terms. Topics run from yards, train callers, and safety to pay rolls, wrecks, and block signals. Other letters deal with hiring, school for staff, letters and wires, and unions. The tone stays warm, but the advice is firm and based on long use.
45111-the-anglo-saxon-century-and-the-un:
Anglo Saxon Century, by John Dos Passos of the New York bar, urges union. Putnam issued the second edition in nineteen o three in New York and London. Its full aim is the joining of the English speaking peoples as one. Dos Passos had written on stock exchanges and on commercial trusts.

The survey opens with two events that mark the nineteenth century close. The Spanish War, he argues, changed the place of America in the world. War in Africa likewise shifted the power and ties of England then. Chapters map Russia, China, and France against that new world scene. The form of a proposed alliance is then weighed at length.
45744-catalogue-of-the-gallery-of-art-of:
Catalogue of the Gallery of Art of the New-York Historical Society was printed for the Society in New York in 1915. The front pages list the Society's officers and executive committee, led by President John Abeel Weekes. Librarian Robert Kelby kept the collections that the gallery displayed.

Inside, the catalogue records the paintings and other works held in the gallery at that date. Such lists fixed what a museum owned, where taste stood, and which artists mattered to the city. Collectors, artists, and visitors could check a work against the printed page. Today the volume also serves as a snapshot of an old New York institution and the art it prized in 1915.
46007-our-young-aeroplane-scouts-in-russ:
Horace Porter wrote Our Young Aeroplane Scouts in Russia. A L Burt Company issued it at New York in 1915. Its subtitle tells of boys lost on the frozen steppes. Billy Barry and Henri Trouville fly as the scouts. Porter wrote sister books for France, Germany, and Turkey. A great airship at a mile a minute fronts the book.

The Warsaw aviation chief greets the boys in chapter one. They were lost in Petrograd, he jokes at them. Special messengers praise their fast return, he adds. Colonel Malinkoff chose them as pilots for the work. The Sign of the Thumb heads that first chapter. War work for boy airmen fills the tale that follows. Early Great War flying fiction put American boys in allied cockpits while their own country still stood neutral.
46356-the-toxicity-of-caffein-an-experim:
William Salant and J B Rieger wrote The Toxicity of Caffein, a lab study on many kinds of animals. The Bureau of Chemistry issued it as Bulletin One Hundred Forty Eight in nineteen hundred twelve. The Government Printing Office in Washington printed the work. H W Wiley, chief of the bureau, sent it forth.

Food and drug law work drove the tests in the lab. Salant ran the drug lab of the bureau at the time. Rabbits took the drug by skin, mouth, vein, and gut in turn. Guinea pigs, cats, and dogs each got their own full rounds. Sharp one dose harm and slow long use both get weighed. Cut open checks by John R Mohler’s men back the dose tales. First claims stay marked as trial in Wiley’s note. The sum of the work fills the last pages with care.
46370-british-flags-their-early-history-:
British Flags is a study by Perrin, printed at Cambridge in 1922. Perrin served as Admiralty Librarian and secretary of the Navy Records Society. Vaughan drew the colour pictures. The Cambridge Naval and Military Series carried it, under editors Corbett and Edwards.

The subtitle promises the early history of flags and their growth at sea. It also traces the flag as a national device. Chapters open with the flag's origin up to the thirteenth century. Later chapters treat early English, Scottish, and Irish flags, then the union flags and jacks. Flags of command and colours of distinction follow. Perrin gives sailors and historians the flag's story in full.
47039-botany-for-ladies-or-a-popular-int:
Botany for Ladies, or a Popular Introduction to the Natural System of Plants, is a work by Mrs Loudon, printed at London in 1842. It follows the classification of De Candolle, and Loudon also wrote Instructions in Gardening for Ladies. Her preface is a small memoir of learning the science the hard way, as a grown woman who had failed at it as a child.

She tells how the Linnean system repelled her as a girl, its classes and orders impossible to remember. As a wife who walked gardens at her husband's side, she kept asking the names of flowers and feeling her ignorance. Resolving to learn by the natural system instead, she met hard names at the very threshold, and wrote this book to smooth the path for others.
47158-the-matabele-campaign-being-a-narr:
The Matabele Campaign is a narrative of the eighteen ninety six rising in Rhodesia by Baden Powell. Baden Powell served as a major general and fellow of a geographical society. Methuen published the fourth edition in London in nineteen o one. Nearly one hundred pictures, many drawn on the spot, fill its pages.

The author warns that the notes come from his diary and letters home. They were jotted at odd hours, often when sleep would have served better. The campaign spread over a vast country with few and mixed white forces. Supply and transport were its worst trials, little grasped back home. Baden Powell worked first at organising in Buluwayo, then tested it in the field. Scouting, his prized art, fills a long chapter of the book's opening half.
47190-foot-prints-of-a-letter-carrier-or:
Foot Prints of a Letter Carrier, or a History of the World's Correspondence, is a work by James Rees. Rees was a clerk in the Philadelphia post office. The book was issued at Philadelphia in eighteen sixty six. Its subtitle promises biographies, tales, sketches, incidents, and statistics tied to postal history.

A line from Adam Smith on the post office as a mercantile project stands at the front. In his preface Rees says few institutions have a history so little known as the post office. The mere name leads most folk to think they know it, he argues. School books slight the subject, he adds. His aim is to place the post before readers as a key branch of government. Incidents and local matter are woven in to give its social and political history interest.
47273-the-new-york-obelisk-cleopatra-s-n:
Charles E Moldenke wrote this study of the New York obelisk, known as Cleopatra's Needle, published at New York in 1891. The book first gives a sketch of obelisks in general: where they stand, who raised them, and who moved them through the ages.

Later chapters tell how obelisks were quarried, carried, and set up, and what their form and sun-worship meaning were. The last part gives the history of the New York stone and its removal from Alexandria to its new home. Moldenke packs the small book with lists, sizes, and lore. It suits readers who pass the great needle in Central Park and want its long story.
47309-experiments-on-the-nervous-system-:
Alexander Monro ran tests on nerves with opium and with metals. His book came out in Edinburgh in 1793. Monro taught healing, body lore, and surgery at the town's high school of learning. He was a fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. His aim was to learn what animal electricity is.

Frogs ground the first tests on blood flow and nerves. Opium tests show how the drug dulls or stirs the nerves. Metal tests move a fluid in dead limbs, he claims. He then weighs if that fluid is the nerve fluid itself. His verdict sets them apart in the close. Old cure lore fans get a key text.
47337-the-expositor-s-bible-the-general-:
