The General Epistles of Saint James and Saint Jude is a commentary in the Expositor's Bible. Alfred Plummer, master of University College, Durham, wrote the volume here. Robertson Nicoll edited the whole set for Hodder and Stoughton of London. This sixth edition came off the press in the year 1907. Plummer had been fellow and senior tutor at Trinity College, Oxford.

An opening chapter treats the Catholic Epistles as one old set of letters. James and Jude stand first and last in that fifteen-century-old grouping. Chapters test whether the letter of James is truly from his hand. James the brother of the Lord stands forth as its true author. The Jews of the dispersion are named as those first addressed in it. Links to Paul, Peter, Ecclesiasticus, and Wisdom get weighed in turn. Joy in temptation and the fading rich fill the doctrine chapters.
48753-ten-acres-enough-a-practical-exper:
Ten Acres Enough, here in its eighth edition from James Miller of New York in 1866, reports one man's practical trial of small farming. Its full title promises to show how a very small farm may be made to keep a very large family, with profitable experience in growing the smaller fruits.

The preface scolds the common ambition to own more land than a farmer can manure or work well, and measures the mistake in wasted labour. The author writes instead for city, town, and village workers who long to leave the desk, the counter, or the workshop for a moderate but sure income in the country. Few books of plain farming experience existed for such readers, and this one became their guide.
48887-the-month-of-mary-according-to-the:
The Month of Mary, according to the spirit of Saint Francis of Sales, is a devotional book by Don Caspar Gilli. It holds thirty-one considerations with examples and prayers, one for each day. A sister of the Institute of Charity translated and shortened it from the Italian. It was printed at London in 1890 with the church's approval.

The days move through Mary's life and virtues. The eve of the month treats the Immaculate Conception. The first day shows Mary as a model of perfect self-denial from her birth, and the sixth day treats the Annunciation. Each day pairs its meditation with an example: the miraculous medal, the feasts of Mary, or the love of a saint for her. Later days treat the Visitation and the charity of Mary in it. The book guides a month of prayer in the Salesian spirit.
49182-the-life-and-letters-of-george-joh:
The Life and Letters of George John Romanes tells a great science worker’s tale. His wife wrote and shaped the book from his own papers and posts. Longmans, Green issued this second edition in eighteen hundred ninety six. She gives it to their children as a record of their sire.

Romanes was born at Kingston in Canada on May twentieth, eighteen hundred forty eight. His father taught Greek at the small college of that town. Old Scots kin in Berwickshire stood behind the learned house. Sweet temper and calm ways marked the son through all his life. Youth, London, and the Geanies years fill the first three parts. Oxford days from eighteen hundred ninety to ninety four close the span. Tales that his mind failed near death are false, his wife writes. Professor Burdon Sanderson’s notice backs her word in full.
49327-labors-in-the-vineyard-twelfth-boo:
Labors in the Vineyard is the twelfth book of the Faith Promoting Series, published at the Juvenile Instructor office in Salt Lake City in 1884. The series was designed for the instruction and encouragement of young Latter day Saints. Its books were used in many Sunday schools and read eagerly by young people across Utah Territory, the publisher says.

The stories tell the experiences of Mormon missionaries, the faithful elders of the preface. Some incidents are so miraculous, the publisher warns, that readers will exclaim that truth is stranger than fiction. The first narrative, My Experience in England, begins with a call to a mission. The elder travels through deep snow to the Platte River and procures a new outfit for the road.
49362-helpful-visions-the-fourteenth-boo:
Helpful Visions gathers faith tales for young Latter-day Saints. It is the fourteenth book of the Faith-Promoting Series. The Juvenile Instructor office at Salt Lake City put it out in 1887. Its stated aim is to teach and hearten the young of that church. Short lives and strange events fill its pages in turn.

David Kimball tells of a hard ordeal and spirit signs he saw. A search for a lost father fills the next tale in the book. Briant Stevens, a boy who won four lads to baptism, stands next. His hurts, his priesthood, and his early death close that sad life. A vision of comfort comes to his grieving father in grief. A mission tale to the far south seas ends the set.
49432-the-myth-of-the-manuscript-found-o:
Elder George Reynolds wrote The Myth of the Manuscript Found, the eleventh book of the Faith-Promoting Series. The Juvenile Instructor office published it at Salt Lake City in 1883. The series was designed for the instruction and encouragement of young Latter-day Saints.

Reynolds takes up the famous Spaulding story, the claim that the Book of Mormon was copied from a lost novel. His contents march through the claim point by point: the history of the manuscript, a bogus affidavit, and the speculations of a woman named Dickenson. He then sets out what the Book of Mormon really is, in the church's account. Joseph Smith's early life, the finding of the plates, and the three witnesses all get chapters. The book is early Mormon apologetics, written to arm young readers against a popular attack.
49710-representative-english-comedies-v-:
Representative English Comedies, volume one, gathers early English comedy with essays and notes by many scholars. Charles Mills Gayley of California edited the whole work for Macmillan. The volume runs from the beginnings of English comedy up to Shakespeare. It was first set up in nineteen o three and reprinted in nineteen twenty six.

Each dramatist gets a critical essay and an edited play with full notes. Heywood's Play of the Wether and Johan Johan open the series of texts. Udall's Roister Doister, Stevenson's Gammer Gurton's Needle, and Lyly follow in order. Peele's Old Wives' Tale and Greene's Friar Bacon carry the line forward. Porter's Two Angry Women of Abington is the last play printed. Dowden closes the volume with an essay on Shakespeare as a comic dramatist.
49842-the-rise-and-fall-of-anarchy-in-am:
McLean wrote this subscription book of 1888, The Rise and Fall of Anarchy in America, from its first stirrings to the first bomb thrown in Chicago; the head gives his initials only. The contents promise a full account of the great conspiracy ending in the Haymarket massacre of May 4, 1886. A minute account follows of the arrest, trial, conviction, and execution of the leading conspirators. Order is heaven's first law, the motto runs.

Chapters treat the anarchists' nationality, their first agitation, the revenge circular, and the Haymarket meeting. The trial chapters parade bombs in court, detectives, and cross-examination, with Parsons swearing he will not eat snowballs next winter. The front picture is Liberty Enlightening the World. It is the prosecution's story, sold door to door in the hangings' shadow.
50914-dreadnoughts-of-the-dogger-a-story:
Dreadnoughts of the Dogger is a story of the war on the North Sea by Robert Leighton, printed at London and Melbourne in 1916. Leighton also wrote The Golden Galleon and The Thirsty Sword. Thirty-five chapters carry the tale from the Silver Pit to a last meeting on the cliff.

Chapter heads promise watchers of the sea, the menace of mines, a fleet in hiding, and a German admiral. A boy hero named Mark threads through the action, finding secrets in a pigeon loft and making himself small where he should not be. The foe's boat U50 does its worst crime late in the book. The tale gives boys a home-front war of spies, mines, and big ships.
51886-down-at-caxton-s:
Walter Lecky wrote Down at Caxton's, a set of sketches printed at Baltimore in 1895. Lecky, author of Adirondack Sketches, says the pieces were done at odd moments stolen from the busy life of a country doctor in the wildest part of the Adirondacks. He dedicated the book to his friend Charles Warren Stoddard.

The sketches profile writers of his day, sorted under men and women. Among them are Richard Malcolm Johnston, Marion Crawford, Agnes Repplier, and Louise Imogen Guiney. A closing piece takes up literature and the Catholic poor. Lecky writes as an insider of the Catholic literary world of the 1890s, and the book preserves warm, personal portraits of authors now little read.
51959-bill-nye-and-boomerang-or-the-tale:
Bill Nye and Boomerang is a book of humour by Bill Nye, printed at Chicago in 1883. Its subtitle calls it the tale of a meek-eyed mule, and some other literary gems. The volume is dedicated, cheerfully and even hilariously, to the author's mule Boomerang, whose bright smile haunts him still. A verse from the Sweet Singer of Michigan fronts the dedication.

In an apology dated November 1880, Nye sends his publishers the matter for a medium size volume of his writings. He owns that the pieces were arranged in a hurry. So he has hurried to fill the gap. The book gathers the sketches that made him the best known humorist of the American West in his day.
51999-life-and-military-career-of-major-:
Life and Military Career of William Tecumseh Sherman, by Headley, was published in New York in 1865. Appleton issued the book while the Civil War still ran. Headley had written lives of Napoleon and Josephine. His preface owns that Sherman's career had just reached its brightest period. Facts of the early life came from those who knew the general best. Colonel Bowman's sketches in a service magazine supplied much. The Army and Navy Journal lent more.

An unpublished pen-portrait by Alvord is promised as a prize. Headley offers annals, not a sifted biography: incidents and movements in order. Youth, he hopes, will take fire from the example. The book closes as a debt of thanks for a preserved Union. It catches Sherman's fame at the moment of the March to the Sea.
52412-abraham-lincoln-and-the-abolition-:
Charles Godfrey Leland wrote a life of Abraham Lincoln for the Makers of History set, with rights held from 1879. Caldwell of New York issued this second edition, with a few dates and names set right. Leland wrote the book while he lived abroad, away from his best sources.

He makes no plea for adding one more life. Such an example of hard work and truth, he says, can not be shown too much to young men. Lincoln's rule was, in his view, the life of the land itself. The tale runs from a boy's first school and self-teaching to the war years and the end of slavery.
52728-bell-s-cathedrals-st-david-s:
Philip Robson's The Cathedral Church of Saint David's, in Bell's Cathedral Series, was published in London in 1901 by George Bell and Sons, with fifty illustrations. Robson calls it a short history and description of the fabric and the bishop's buildings. He gives the book to the memory of Dean James Allen, the church's most careful custodian.

His preface owns the book is a digest of larger works, above all the history by Jones and Freeman. Visitors get plain advice: St David's is hard to reach, so sleep at Haverfordwest and drive the sixteen miles and seventeen hills next day. The pictures are mostly his own photographs, with measured drawings reduced from prize plans of 1882.
52811-anarchy-and-anarchists-a-history-o:
Michael Schaack's Anarchy and Anarchists, published at Chicago in 1889, is a police captain's history of the red terror. Its full title promises communism, socialism, and nihilism in doctrine and in deed, in America and Europe. The center of the book is the Chicago Haymarket conspiracy and the detection and trial of the conspirators. Schaack dedicates the volume to Joseph Gary and Julius Grinnell, the judge and prosecutor of that trial.

In the preface Schaack pledges fairness under the motto, nothing extenuate, nor set down aught in malice. He says he tried to stand in the place of the men whose conspiracy led to the Haymarket explosion and the gallows. His duty after the bomb, as he states it, was to bring the guilty to justice and expose the plot. The broader history of the movements frames the Chicago story.
53465-lessons-in-the-small-catechism-of-:
Mezger, a professor at Concordia Seminary in Saint Louis, wrote Lessons in the Small Catechism of Martin Luther, printed in Saint Louis in 1923 by Concordia Publishing House. The lessons serve the senior department of Lutheran Sunday schools, and general use as well. Lesson one treats the catechism and the Bible together.

Mezger explains that the word catechism means instruction, and that this little book gives instruction in a brief and simple form a child can grasp. It teaches what every Christian should know, in Luther's own short questions and answers, opened up by a teacher. Lutheran families and schools used such books for generations of confirmation training.
53663-sweet-p-s:
Sweet P's, by Julie Lippmann, was published at Philadelphia in 1902. Ida Waugh drew the pictures. Lippmann had written Miss Wildfire and Dorothy Day. She gives the book to her little friend Natalie Wilson. Twelve chapters trace two girls, Priscilla and Polly. Chapter one is called Miss Cissy's Plan. It opens on Priscilla's eighth birthday. Hannah the nurse sets her in a big chair in her best frock. She must not stir and rumple it before the company.

Priscilla is a quiet only child with solemn brown eyes. Kin call her a poor little thing, while the maids call her lucky and rich. She puzzles over how both can be true. Chapter heads promise a party, a telegram, and victories for each girl.
53895-christmas-at-mccarthy-s:
Edna Randolph Worrell wrote entertainments and songs sold by the Paine Publishing Company of Dayton, Ohio, at twenty five cents each. New entertainment songs by Worrell are advertised at the front. The music is easy, and both music and words are especially catchy, the notice says. Children like them, and everybody likes them. Five copies go for a dollar.

We Hope You've Brought Your Smiles Along is a welcome song that puts an audience in a joyous frame at once, the list promises. A happy first impression means half the success of your entire program. We'll Now Have to Say Good Bye has snap and go to send an audience home with happy memories. We've Just Arrived from Bashful Town recalls bashful school days. My Own America, I Love Thee brings a thrill of patriotism. School and church Christmas programs ran on such pieces.
53932-frank-reade-jr-and-his-new-steam-m:
Frank Reade Junior and His New Steam Man belongs to the Frank Reade Library, the famous dime novel series of the eighteen nineties. The steam man was a robot of iron, driven by steam, shaped like a man, and built to haul the young inventor's wagon across the plains. Noname, the series' house name, wrote the tales.

Frank Reade Junior, son of the inventor of the first steam man, builds machines beyond his father's: airships, submarines, and electric wonders after this one. The stories run on chases, fights, and last minute escapes in the wild west and beyond. The Frank Reade books were the science fiction of the dime novel age. Boys read them under the covers by the million. The steam man himself became an icon of early robot dreams.
54369-the-romance-of-madame-tussaud-s:
John Theodore Tussaud wrote a history of Madame Tussaud's waxworks, copyrighted in 1920, with an introduction by Hilaire Belloc. A portrait shows Madame Tussaud at the age of eighty five. The author says his wife's urging grew these leaves into a book. Chapter one enters his father's studio and traces Madame's birth and parentage.

Her uncle Curtius left medicine for art and moved from Berne to Paris. Life size figures were shown at the Palais Royal and on the Boulevard du Temple. Benjamin Franklin and Voltaire sat for figures. Madame went to Versailles before the revolution. Later chapters cover the twelfth of July 1789 and heads taken from the guillotine era.
54627-the-scripture-club-of-valley-rest-: The Scripture Club of Valley Rest, or sketches of everybody's life, is a humorous village tale in sketches. Its front pages in this copy are the publisher's lists of travel books by other hands, so the tale itself must be met by its title. A scripture club in a restful valley, and sketches of the life of everybody there, is the whole promise of the title page. Such books of the time made gentle comedy of chapel folk, their readings, and their small vanities and kindnesses.
55288-hepplestall-s:
Harold Brighouse wrote Hepplestall's, a novel printed in New York in 1922. Reuben's seal opens the book, in the days when a man might still be a Jacobite for odd reasons. Young Reuben Hepplestall is one from spite: Sir Harry Whitworth is Hanoverian, so Reuben takes the Stuart side to cross him.

His game is risky, yet it feeds his pride: he wins a place in the inner councils of the local Jacobites and savours the danger of it. A tale of love, plot, and a seal runs through the parts. Fans get a sly, warm tale of pride and politics in the north of England.
55429-social-life-in-the-reign-of-queen-:
A study of social life in the reign of Queen Anne, built from original sources, makes up this book. The opening pages plunge straight into the sources themselves: an issue of The Daily Courant from March 1702. News from Naples, Rome, Vienna, and Portugal fills the columns, with troops on the move and courts in stir. Such papers were how Londoners learned the world.

By printing the raw material of the age, the book lets readers feel daily life as it was lived and read at the time. War news, court gossip, and small items sit side by side, as they did for Anne's subjects. The method suits the title: social history drawn from the record, not retold at a distance. Students of the early 1700s get sources and story together.
55568-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Pennsylvania Prison Society issued its journal for 1919 as number 58 of the new series, from the Forrest Building in Philadelphia. The volume carries the report of the acting committee, a report of the commission sent to investigate prison systems, and matter on military discipline and punishments.

It opens with the law on prison visiting. The Act of April 23, 1829 names the official visitors, from the Governor and the judges down to county commissioners and sheriffs. The mayors and recorders of Philadelphia, Lancaster, and Pittsburgh stand on the list as well. An Act of March 20, 1903 then made the visiting committees of prison societies official visitors too, with the same powers as the older list.
55576-mogg-s-cab-fare-distance-map-and-l:
Mogg's Cab Fare and Distance Map and Guide to London comes with this index to the streets, squares, and cab stands contained in it, published by Mogg of High Street, Bloomsbury. The index contains three thousand places, with references to their several situations. An explanation sets out the method: the plan is divided into squares, with letters at top and bottom and figures down the sides. To find a place, look it up in the index for its letter and figure, then find that square on the plan.

The example given is St Paul's Church-yard, found at I 8. Before street atlases, Mogg's maps told Londoners what a cab ride should cost. Cab fare disputes were a daily quarrel, and the map settled them.
55765-the-faery-queen-and-her-knights-st:
Alfred J Church, a clergyman known for retelling Homer, turned Edmund Spenser's great poem The Faerie Queene into prose tales for younger readers. The book came out at New York in 1909, with color pictures. Spenser's long verse epic of knights and ladies is here told in clear, simple chapters.

Readers follow the Red-Cross Knight, the lady Una, and the wizard Archimago. They meet Prince Arthur, the giant Orgoglio, and the dragon that must be slain. Later tales tell of Sir Guyon, the warrior maid Britomart, and Artegall. Church keeps the wonder and the moral shape of the poem while making it easy to read.
55790-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang of October 1920 is an issue of a humour magazine from Robbinsdale, Minnesota. The number is volume two, number thirteen, and the editor calls it the annual. An open letter from the Whiz Bang Farm greets the readers.

The editor celebrates a first birthday survived. The magazine, he writes, has weathered the colicky stage of infancy, cut its eye-teeth, and spread from Manhattan to California on jokes sent in by readers. Many stories and poems from the twelve previous issues are reviewed in this number. The motto is to make it snappy, and the tone matches. Farm humour papers of this kind fed jokes to vaudeville and radio. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
55946-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang, volume two, number sixteen, came out in January 1921 as a monthly of jokes and verse from Fawcett, its publisher. The motto on the cover orders all hands to make it snappy. The issue opens with a poem by Whiz Bang Bill called Keep On Keepin' On, a dose of cheer for a gloomy day.

If the day looks kind of gloomy and chances kind of slim, the verse bids the reader bristle up, grit his teeth, and keep on. Inside come the usual jokes, farmer humor, and short verse that made the Whiz Bang a farm belt hit. Readers get small town America laughing at itself in the first years after the war.
56307-awdeley-s-fraternitye-of-vacabonde:
Awdeleys Fraternity of Vagabonds and Harmans Caueat hold old tracts on rogue life. An early English text society put the rare prints out in one book. Editors Viles and Furnivall set the texts from old copies in great vaults. The set bears the year eighteen sixty nine on its title page.

One tract lists the ranks and tricks of beggar folk in old England. Harmans warn book adds cant terms and tales of knave craft at large. A sermon by a parson named Haben is bound in the same set. Notes set side by side the variant prints of past runs. The book is a chief well for lore of crime speech in old times.
56314-zigzag-journeys-in-the-camel-count:
Samuel Zwemer and Amy Zwemer wrote Zigzag Journeys in the Camel Country, subtitled Arabia in Picture and Story. Revell held the copyright in 1911. The Zwemers had made Topsy-Turvy Land before it, on the same ground.

They dedicate the book to the children of missionaries all the world over. Great parts of Arabia, they warn, remain unknown. Only the camel and his Arab guide have crossed its wide deserts. Travelers and missionaries have seen bits of the coasts and inland tracks. The preface invites big children and small grown-ups to climb aboard. The camels are waiting, it says, and the caravan is ready. Pictures serve as oases along the long desert chapters.
56375-sir-p-s-his-astrophel-and-stella-w:
Astrophel and Stella, printed at London for Thomas Newman in 1591 under the author's initials alone, is a sonnet sequence in the spelling of its day. Its subtitle promises that the excellence of sweet Poesie is concluded in it.

The first sonnet sets the whole design. The lover writes in truth, fain to show his love in verse, so that the dear She may read, reading know, knowing pity, and pity win grace. Sought words come halting out, and the Muse rebukes him: fool, look in thy heart and write. Later sonnets trace love arriving by degrees, and scorn the dainty wits who borrow phrases, since Stella's face alone teaches what love and beauty be.
56911-the-new-century-standard-letter-wr:
Alfred Chambers wrote The New Century Standard Letter-Writer, a manual of model letters for business, family, and social use. Letter-writer books gave forms for every occasion: applications, orders, complaints, invitations, condolences, proposals, and refusals, with rules for addressing envelopes and persons of rank. Chambers's volume brought the old letter-writer up to date for the new century's offices and homes.

Such books taught clerks, immigrants, and young people the forms of written politeness when nearly all business and courtship passed through the mail. The model letters show what the age counted as a proper tone. Whole later books of etiquette grew from this stock.
56968-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-1-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang, volume one, number eleven, is dated August 1920. Fawcett published the monthly at Robbinsdale, Minnesota. The price was 25 cents. Its motto stands on the masthead: Make It Snappy. A Roosevelt line on loyalty to the American people heads the page. The editor was a veteran of the Spanish and World Wars. The little journal is dedicated to the fighting forces of the United States, past, present, and future. An announcement leads: with the October issue the paper starts its second year. A Year Book will gather the best poems, jokes, and stories of the first twelve numbers.

A new series opens in this number: Hollywood Heart-Breakers. It promises the intimate lives of movie folk near Los Angeles. The editor swears it is no press agent dope.
57034-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-ii-n:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang, volume two, number nineteen, dated April 1921, calls itself America's magazine of wit. The joke monthly came from Robbinsdale, Minnesota, and sold by mail for two dollars and fifty cents a year. A short verse on saying hello opens the issue.

Jokes, short verses, and farm-yard fun fill the pages in the style the cover promises. The editor signs himself Whiz Bang Bill, and the tone stays light from start to end. Readers in 1921 bought the magazine for quick laughs, not news. The issue now reads as a sample of small-town American humor between the wars, with its slang and gags kept just as printed.
57050-stavrogin-s-confession-and-the-pla:
F M Dostoevsky's Stavrogin's Confession appears here in English. S S Koteliansky and Virginia Woolf translated it. Leonard and Virginia Woolf issued it at the Hogarth Press in 1922. Their house stood on Paradise Road, Richmond. The plan of The Life of a Great Sinner joins it. Both texts came from Russian government print.

Stavrogin's Confession holds chapters cut from The Possessed. The great sinner novel was planned but never writ. Russian notes by three scholars stand translated here. V Friche and V Komarovich wrote those notes. N Brodsky added a third note to the set. The find's story stands in the government note. A suppressed confession from a great novel reached English in the Woolfs' own press, a landmark of modern letters in a thin paper volume.
57162-a-narrative-of-the-melancholy-wrec:
A sad tale tells how the ship Dunbar was wrecked at Port Jackson. The wreck fell on August 20, 1857, at the South Head. James Johnson was the sole man cast live from the ship. His photo, from Freeman Brothers, fronts this lone-spread form. Verse at the front tells of the wide, dark, wild sea.

No warn was heard, and no help stood at hand that night. The sea took all but one with vast, blind force. Johnson was cast faint on the dire rocks of the shore. Views of the key spots go with the short tale. Sea past fans get a grim, true tale in full.
57177-australia-at-war-a-winter-record-m:
Will Dyson made Australia at War, a winter record of drawings from the Somme and at Ypres during the campaigns of 1916 and 1917. Chesterton wrote the introduction, and the first edition came out in London in 1918. Dyson gave the book to the men of the Australian Imperial Force, in a verse dedication to those who trod that dire road.

Dyson served as an official war artist, and his drawings show tired men, mud, guns, and rest billets with a tender, ironic eye. He drew soldiers as he found them, not as heroes on a poster. Readers get one of the finest picture records of the First World War, made by an Australian for Australians.
57275-the-juvenile-scrap-book-for-1849-a:
The Juvenile Scrap Book for 1849 is a Christmas and New Year's gift book for young people. Grandfather Merryman edited it, and it was issued at New York with twenty-eight engravings on steel. The preface, dated from Philadelphia in December 1848, tells how the editor's granddaughter begged for new tales during a holiday visit.

Stories and lessons fill the pages: The Proud Girl, The Use of Punishments, Julian and his Rabbit, and Lizzie Carson. Faithful Fido and The Carter's Helpmates plead kindness to animals, while Cruelty to Animals and Deception Punished state the moral outright. Harry and his Rabbits, Pussy-hood, and Scenes in the Life of a Roach add lighter fare. Such annuals were stocking gifts of their day, built to amuse and instruct at once.
57389-jeanne-d-arc-maid-of-orleans-deliv:
Douglas Murray edited this life of Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans and deliverer of France, published at London in 1902 with illustrations and a map. Its subtitle promises her story as attested on oath and set forth in the original documents: the record of her trial and rehabilitation. A reputed portrait fronts it, from a painting once at Orleans. The English, the text opens, had felt sorely the humiliations of 1429.

Bedford's report told of soldiers struck with fear by the incantations of this limb of the fiend who had startled them from their security. Proclamations went out against men who deserted in terror of the Maid. Now, betrayed by her own countrymen, she was in English hands, and they wreaked vengeance without stint. Chained, mocked, threatened, and insulted, her serenity never failed. The book rests on the trial record itself.
57808-the-englishwoman-in-italy-impressi:
The Englishwoman in Italy is a travel and society book by Mrs Gretton. Hurst and Blackett published it in London. Its subtitle calls it impressions of life in the Roman States and Sardinia. Those impressions come from a ten years' residence in Italy. The contents open with a departure from Florence by vettura. An inn among the Apennines and decaying Romagna towns follow. Austrian officers at Forli and dangers of the road are noted.

First impressions of Ancona close the first chapter's heads. A palazzo and complimentary visits of the nobility fill chapter two. The Anconitans dislike country walks, the heads observe. A marriage in high life gets the third chapter. Wedding outfits and the laws of courtship are set out there. The condition of single women is treated in that chapter. Gretton writes as a long resident watching Italian society.
58183-haworth-s:
Haworth's, a novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett, was published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1907, from a copyright of 1879 renewed in 1907. Burnett also wrote That Lass o' Lowrie's, another tale of working life. The book stands among her early, serious novels, before her fame for children's stories.

Chapter heads span long stretches of time: Twenty Years, Thirty Years, Not Finished. The story turns on the Haworth works and the people bound up with them. Janey appears among the early figures. Mill town labour, pride, and endurance give the tale its weight. The novel shows the strain between owners and hands in an industrial town.
58274-the-tragic-story-of-the-empress-of:
The Tragic Story of the Empress of Ireland, by Logan Marshall, is disaster reportage. Myers held the rights in 1914 for this swift, photo filled account. The liner left Quebec for Liverpool with over thirteen hundred souls aboard her. The collier Storstad struck her off Father Point on May 29, 1914.

She sank in about fifteen minutes, with some one thousand lives lost. Captains Kendall and Andersen give rival statements of blame in print here. Survivor lists and a roll of the dead fill a long grim chapter. Salvation Army losses and heroes of the night get their own sections. The Titanic tale and other sea disasters fill the second half.
584-our-nig-or-sketches-from-the-life-of:
A Black woman writing as Our Nig tells of Frado, a free Black girl bound out to a white New England family, in this early American novel. Frado, deserted by kin and frail in health, works in a two-story white house where her mistress, steeped in Southern ways, treats her with cruelty. Slavery's shadows, the title warns, fall even in the North.

The preface confesses the writer's plain style and her need to earn a living for herself and her child. She spares neither her own faults nor her mistress's. The book stands as a pioneering Black American narrative, frank about Northern racism and a girl's fight to keep her spirit whole.
58495-secrets-of-meat-curing-and-sausage:
Heller and Company, manufacturing chemists of Chicago, published Secrets of Meat Curing and Sausage Making. This fifth edition is dated December 1922. The title page invites visitors to inspect the factory on Calumet Avenue, and promises a pleased welcome.

The book tells how to cure hams, shoulders, bacon, and corned beef. It tells how to make all kinds of sausage. Its methods are framed to comply with the pure food laws, as the title boasts. The long index runs from the age for killing stock to the firm's own preparations, with names like Aseptifume and Ant-Bane. Trade books of this kind were catalogs in disguise, but they also carried real craft: salt, smoke, spice, and time, set down for butchers and farmers who cured their own meat.
58819-the-choir-school-of-st-bede-s:
The Choir School of Saint Bede's is a school story by Frederick Harrison. Blackie and Son published it in London, Glasgow, and Bombay. Emily Cook drew its thirteen illustrations. 

The story opens in the cloister of a grand old cathedral church. The choir boys are at play on the grass between school hours. One boy of about eleven stands shyly apart by a stone pillar. He is Alfred Davidson, the new probationer solo-boy of the choir. A bigger boy cross-questions him about his home and his father. His father, it comes out, is an engineer on a ship bound for Australia. Chapters ahead promise an April fool's day, a paper-chase, and a visit to the deanery.
59044-tales-of-english-minsters-st-paul-:
Elizabeth Grierson wrote Tales of English Minsters: St Paul's, printed in London in 1910. It holds two colour plates and four in black and white. A view of St Paul's from Ludgate Hill fronts it. The set runs to Durham, Lincoln, York, Ely, and Canterbury as well. Grierson was known for a children's book of Edinburgh.

Signing Magna Charta in colour and preaching at Paul's Cross in black and white show the tale's range. The cathedral's story runs from the old church of the Saxons through fire, Wren's dome, and the life of London round it. Saints, kings, and choristers fill its chapels. Young readers get a great church by its stories.
59663-notes-on-diseases-of-swine-sheep-p:
Notes on Diseases of Swine, Sheep, Poultry and the Dog is a handbook by Korinek. The Veterinary Science Association issued it, with copyright in 1917. Korinek was a graduate of the Ontario college. He had served as Oregon's state veterinarian. Sixteen years of practice stand behind the notes. Four chapters divide the book by kind of beast. Swine come first, then sheep and goats.

Poultry follow, and the dog closes the set. Each chapter gives cause, signs, and treatment. A chart names the parts of each animal. Plain words are used on purpose, the preface says. Students and working vets are the readers aimed at. Farm men could use it at the pen side. Such handbooks spread animal doctoring widely.
59700-american-masters-of-sculpture-bein:
Charles Caffin's American Masters of Sculpture, copyrighted in 1903 and reissued by Doubleday, Page in 1913, gives brief appreciations of American sculptors. The Sherman Monument by Augustus Saint-Gaudens fronts the book. Caffin had already done the same work for painting in a companion volume.

Saint-Gaudens takes the first and longest place, with his Grief, his Lincoln, and his relief portrait of Robert Louis Stevenson in the plates. Chapters follow on George Grey Barnard, Ward, Daniel Chester French, and MacMonnies, then Bartlett, Herbert Adams, Niehaus, Warner, Borglum, and Brenner. Two closing chapters step back to weigh the decorative motive and the ideal motive in the art.
60229-the-priest-and-the-acolyte-with-an:
The Priest and the Acolyte is a short story reprinted at London by the Lotus Press in 1907, with an introductory protest by Stuart Mason. The edition exists to correct a fraud. So many copies, the publisher says, had been sold under the implication that the story was Oscar Wilde's work that a true edition was needed to end the deception.

The story first appeared in The Chameleon, whose first and only number came out in December 1894. Its author was an Oxford undergraduate, who alone was responsible for the magazine he edited. At the Queensberry libel trial a few months later, an attempt was made to show that Wilde approved the story's theme and shared in its publication. This edition prints the tale with the record set straight. The story itself, of a priest and his acolyte, remains a dark relic of the eighteen-nineties.
60562-the-greatest-plague-of-life-or-the:
The Greatest Plague of Life, or the adventures of a lady in search of a good servant, was edited by the brothers Mayhew and pictured by George Cruikshank. David Bogue of Fleet Street published it in London. The author hides behind a plain label: one who has been almost worried to death. A frontispiece shows the lady nearly worried to death by the plagues of her life.

The introduction asks why women, born to suffer, must also carry the troubles of men. Without a woman to soothe and look after him, the writer argues, man would go about like a brute, robbed right and left by his servants. The chapters then march through the search: cooks, maids, and helps of every temper. The comedy rests on a grievance every mistress of a house then knew well.
60629-sketches-of-the-war-a-series-of-le:
Sketches of the War is a series of letters by Charles C Nott. Anson D F Randolph published this third edition in New York in 1865. Nott, a captain in the Fifth Iowa Cavalry, was also a New York school trustee. The letters were addressed to the North Moore Street School. Nott inscribes them to William B Eager Jr, a faithful school officer.

The sketches follow the western war. The Hospital opens the series, and Donelson follows. The Assault, Foraging, and A Flag of Truce come next. The Holly Fork, Scouting, and A Surprise fill the middle. The Escape and The Last Scout close the ten letters. The preface to the second edition explains the book's charity. That edition was published for the exclusive benefit of disabled soldiers. Nott wrote the letters amid the scenes they describe. He avoided baby-talk, he says, and trusted children with real writing.
60831-between-heathenism-and-christianit:
Between Heathenism and Christianity, published in 1899, joins translations of two classical works. Seneca's De Providentia stands beside Plutarch's essay on the delay of divine justice. The translator is Charles W Super, a former president of Ohio University and its professor of Greek. Notes and further extracts accompany the texts. Two essays of Super's own, on Greek and Roman life in the first century after Christ, complete the volume.

Super's preface argues that the rise and rapid spread of Christianity is the most striking fact in recorded history. He sets the two pagan writers beside that rise. Both asked how a just providence governs a world of suffering, and both answered without knowledge of the spreading faith. The book invites readers to measure the best of pagan thought against the new religion.
60989-the-geology-of-d-a-r-state-park-mt:
Geology of three Vermont state parks is a survey by Harry Dodge for the Vermont Geological Survey. The parks are the DAR State Park, Mount Philo State Forest Park, and Sand Bar State Park. The survey issued the book at Montpelier in 1969 under the state geologist, Charles Doll. It was a joint issue of the departments of forests and parks and of water resources.

Plates at the front show the shoreline at the DAR park looking south in a photograph. A panoramic view from the west overlook on Mount Philo shows the Adirondacks across Lake Champlain in another. Sand Bar park stands on the flat surface of the Lamoille river delta in its plate. Such guidebooks taught the park visitor to read the shore: old beaches, lake clays, and the rocks of the Champlain valley under the picnic ground.
61115-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-2-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang was a monthly magazine of wit, humor, and what it called filosophy. This issue is volume two, number twenty-three, dated August 1921. Fawcett put it out from Robbinsdale, Minnesota, for twenty-five cents a copy. Fawcett, a veteran of the Spanish and World Wars, edited it for fellow fighting men.

Jokes, short verse, and comic bits fill the pages, mixed with ads. Readers could buy photos, books of war cartoons, and subscriptions to an army paper. A column called Drippings From the Fawcett opens the fun. The tone is barracks humor of the post-war years, aimed at men who had served overseas and now read for laughs at home.
61435-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-3-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang was a Minnesota joke magazine, sold as America's magazine of wit and humor from a farm address at Robbinsdale. This file holds the October 1921 number, volume three, number twenty-five. Advertisements for photographs of California bathing girls crowd the opening pages.

Captain Billy Fawcett, a wounded veteran turned publisher, built the Whiz Bang from a mimeographed sheet for soldiers into a national success. Farmyard filosophy and foolishness, as the coupon spells it, mix jokes, verses, and small-town sass. The magazine's cheerful vulgarity scandalized ministers and sold hugely at barbershops and newsstands. This issue shows the formula in its prime, ads, coupons, jokes and all.
62141-an-earnest-exhortation-to-a-freque:
An Earnest Exhortation to a Frequent Reception of the Holy Sacrament of the Lord's Supper is a small tract by a layman, in a seventh edition printed in London in 1811. It was sold at three pence, or half a crown a dozen, for wide giving away. The piece is addressed particularly to young persons.

The author says he can hope to say nothing new on so great a subject. His aim is to take the objections young persons make for staying away from the sacrament and answer them in a new point of view, in a few pages. The tract began as a letter to a gentleman who had told him his scruples. Brevity and plain speech are its tools, in the style of the tract societies of its day.
62279-captain-billy-s-whiz-bang-vol-3-no:
Captain Billy's Whiz Bang for January nineteen twenty-two is volume three, number twenty-nine of the magazine. W H Fawcett published it each month at Robbinsdale, Minnesota, at twenty-five cents a copy. The cover calls it America's magazine of wit, humour, and philosophy.

The issue pushes the Winter Annual, Pedigreed Follies of nineteen twenty-one to twenty-two. That bound book holds two hundred and fifty-six pages of jokes, jests, jingles, and stories. Last year's annual, the ad warns, sold out on the Pacific Coast in days. Readers are told to pin a dollar bill to the coupon and mail it fast. A line from Theodore Roosevelt heads the issue.
62693-climate-and-time-in-their-geologic:
Climate and Time in their Geological Relations is a theory of slow changes in the earth's climate by James Croll of the Geological Survey of Scotland, issued at London in 1875. Its front picture shows the northern winter turning point in two positions of the earth's path. In his preface Croll states his aim plainly. He has tried to give a full and tight statement of the facts and arguments for the theory, he writes.

Much of the volume had appeared in substance as separate papers over the past ten or twelve years, he adds. The theory, above all in its bearing on the cause of the glacial epoch, is slowly winning acceptance with geologists, he notes. The growing knowledge of drift, the rubble the ice left behind, has driven that change. Croll's ice age, driven by shifts in the earth's orbit, now bears his name in science.
63254-the-heritage-of-the-south-a-histor:
Jubal Early wrote The Heritage of the South, a history of the introduction of slavery and its final effect on the politics of the United States, copyrighted in 1915 at Lynchburg, Virginia. Early had sat in the Virginia convention of 1861 and led Confederate troops in the war. His book is a defense of the South's course, made by one of its actors.

The African slave trade and the origin of slavery in the United States open the work. State laws on the question follow, then the causes leading to secession and the going out of the cotton states. The action of the border states and the right to withdraw close the case. Come now, let us reason together, says the motto. Historians read the book as the Lost Cause case in an old general's own words.
66079-free-opinions-freely-expressed-on-:
Marie Corelli, a famed novelist of her day, set down her frank views on modern social life in a set of essays issued in London in 1905. Ads for new six shilling novels fill the first leaf, then her own sharp pen takes over. The essays had run as social papers in the press before they were bound.

Heads of the parts show her range: the charge of the press, pagan London, a question of faith, and unchristian clerics. She strikes at the blight of high life, the death of hospitality, and the coarseness of new wealth. American women in England, the advance of woman, mad dress, and the decay of home life all get plain words. Work, prayer, and the soul of the nation close the book.
6613-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
On the Pacific slope, Skinner listens to Native spirits of the Northwest, where each tree has a soul and mountains hold guardian powers. The voyager of the Whulge, Tamanous of Tacoma, and the devil at the Dalles open a set that runs down the Columbia to Death Valley and the American Shaft. When Tacoma's spirits fought Hood's, fire and melted stone burst from the peaks.

Hunger Valley, Misery Hill, and Bridal Veil Fall add human sorrow to the spirit world. Skinner treats these tales with respect, as living lore, not mere fancy. On the Pacific Slope is a vivid, short tour of western myth, where land and spirit are one.
66135-three-visitors-to-early-plymouth-l:
Three Visitors to Early Plymouth holds letters about the Pilgrim settlement in New England during its first seven years. Sydney V James Junior shaped the book, and Samuel Eliot Morison wrote the opening. Plimoth Plantation printed it in 1963. A map of New England about 1625 stands at the front.

The writers are John Pory, Emmanuel Altham, and Isaack de Rasieres. Pory letters go to the Earl of Southampton on January 13, 1622 and 1623, and to the governor of Virginia in autumn 1622. Altham writes to his brother Edward in September 1623, March 1624, and June 1625, and to James Sherley in May 1624. De Rasieres writes to Samuel Blommaert about 1628. The editor gave modern spelling without changing the words. History fans get the Pilgrims through fresh outside eyes.
66181-secret-history-of-to-day-being-rev:
Allen Upward wrote Secret History of To-Day, billed as the tales of a diplomatic spy. G P Putnam’s Sons issued the book in New York and London in nineteen hundred four. Upward had written Secrets of the Courts of Europe before. The Kaiser in winged helmet fronts the book in state.

The telegram that began the Boer War leads his twelve tales. The blowing up of the Maine comes next in his list of plots. Captain Dreyfus and his long mystery fill the third long part. What lay back of the Tsar’s peace call gets its own probe. King Humbert’s true killer and Queen Draga’s death crowd in. Norway’s peril and a Dowager Empress’s ruse stand in turn. Edward the Seventh’s state craft and the Black Pope close the spy’s claims.
668-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words beginning with S. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from S, the sibilant letter, through Saadh, Saan, and Sabadilla, and onward. Notes trace Latin, Greek, and Phoenician roots and mark obsolete senses.

S opens with its own grammar: the plural -s, the possessive -'s, and the hiss that shapes so many words. Beyond those notes lie sailors, shrubs, and saints, each defined in turn. The slice is a good place to see how one letter carries both the tools of speech and a crowd of things.
67064-the-character-and-happiness-of-the:
William Dealtry, rector of Clapham, preached this funeral sermon at Park Chapel in Chelsea on October 13, 1822, and it was printed at London that year by request. The catalog title is a row of star marks from the title page. The dead man was John Owen, minister of the chapel and one of the secretaries of the British and Foreign Bible Society. Dealtry inscribed the sermon to the society's president, vice presidents, and members.

The theme is the character and happiness of them that die in the Lord, drawn from the book of Revelation. Funeral sermons of the day were part praise, part teaching, and part call to the living. This one honors a man who gave his life to spreading the Bible.
67752-on-building-a-theatre-stage-constr:
Irving Pichel wrote On Building a Theatre in 1920. Theatre Arts Incorporated issued it at New York. The book is Monograph Number One of its line. Its subject is stage build and gear. Small theaters, schools, and town halls are its mark. A photo shows the Beechwood Theatre front.

Contents run from the audience hall to the stage plan. Back-stage workers get their own part. Stage gear and stage lighting follow in turn. Stage machines and settings close the course. A book list waits at the end. Plates show the Teatro Farnese and an Elizabethan stage. The Little Theatre and the Munich Art Theatre stand pictured. Plans of the Berlin Volksbuehne aid the text. A builder's handbook for the little theater wave, it packs pro stage craft into small halls.
67918-little-pilgrim-at-aunt-lou-s:
Little Pilgrim at Aunt Lous is a tale for the young in a pilgrim set. A Sunday school union in Philadelphia put the small book out. Its rights line dates the work to the year eighteen seventy nine. Bessie, the little pilgrim, turns five as the tale opens in spring.

The child rides with her kin to the country home of Aunt Lou for weeks. Her father must leave the next day for his work in town. Kittens in her lap on a barn floor form the front scene of the book. Faith, kin love, and soft country days shape the small tale. The book aims its calm tone at Sunday school shelves for small girls.
67928-the-cruise-of-the-royal-mail-steam:
The Cruise of the Royal Mail Steamer Dunottar Castle Round Scotland on Her Trial Trip was printed at Edinburgh by T and A Constable in 1890. The book came with Sir Donald Currie compliments. John Blair drew views and C Hentschel engraved them, among many artists.

Chapters open concerning the good ship, then in the Firth of Clyde and among the southern Hebrides. In the Sound of Mull and round about Skye follow. Wild Loch Alsh and dark Loch Duich, round Cape Wrath, and a raid on Orkney pace the mid run. Our ship name mother, a day of rest, homeward bound, and in the Firth of Forth close the tale. Plates show the music saloon, a corner of the ladies boudoir, and the smoking room. Ship fans get a mail steamer maiden voyage round the Scots coast.
68081-address-of-hon-theodore-roosevelt-:
Theodore Roosevelt gave this speech at Boston on Saturday, April 27, 1912, and the Senate ordered it printed as a public paper two days later. Roosevelt was then fighting President Taft for control of their party. He opens by saying he is glad to plead his cause in old historic Massachusetts.

His theme sits in the heading: principles, not personalities, are at stake. He says he had answered Taft's attacks the night before and will name Taft now only to show the opposed principles each man stands for. He claims to fight for every good citizen, not for himself. The printed speech is a key record of the fierce 1912 contest that split the Republican Party.
68449-address-of-president-roosevelt-at-:
President Theodore Roosevelt spoke at the laying of the corner stone of the office building of the House of Representatives on Saturday, April 14, 1906. The address was printed at Washington by the Government Printing Office. Over a century ago, he begins, Washington laid the corner stone of the Capitol in wooded wilderness beside the Potomac.

Now great additional buildings are needed for the government's business, proof of the nation's growth in people, wealth, and complex interests. The material problems differ from Washington's time, Roosevelt says, but human nature is the same. He turns to Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress and its man with the muck rake, who could look no way but downward. This speech gave the language its muckraker, aimed at corruption that week in the Senate.
6877-the-head-of-kay-s:
At a boys school, the house called Kay's waits for its cricket side to meet Blackburn's in the final house match. Much turns on Fenn, a player who can bat, bowl, and field in the slips. Jimmy Silver opens the tale by warning his mates that Kay's will win, and the early chapters move between tea, talk, and the low stakes of school sport.

Fenn's fall from favor then drives the story, as he faces exile from the house, a night raid, a dethroned place, and a search for who wronged him. Through dorm fights, dayroom plots, and a last house match, Wodehouse keeps the tone light, and the book closes with Kay's itself changing its name.
68964-sniping-in-france-with-notes-on-th:
Sniping in France, by Major H Hesketh Prichard, treats the training of scouts, observers, and snipers in the First World War. General Lord Horne wrote the foreword. Plates come from Ernest Blaikley and from photos, and the book was printed in Great Britain.

Early chapters trace the birth of sniping and the sniper in the trenches. Later parts tell of the First Army School of Scouting, Observation and Sniping, and its course of work. Tales of snipers and observers fill the mid part, with one foe named Wilibald the Hun. Papers at the back treat care of arms, range work, patrols, and the stalking glass. Soldiers and past buffs get the craft of the hidden marksman in full.
69012-drawing-in-charcoal-and-crayon-for:
Frank Fowler's Drawing in Charcoal and Crayon, for the use of students and schools, came from the Cassell Publishing Company at New York, copyrighted in 1885 by Dunham. A prefatory note says the little volume, with its plates, is designed to prepare students for drawing from life.

Part first covers the materials, the outfit needed, and elementary practice. Part second turns to the manner of working, measurement, and crayon portraits with their hair, drapery and backgrounds, then drawing with the point. Fowler calls charcoal the most available of materials: large effects come quickly, erasure is easy, and the art schools of Europe and America use it for cast and figure. He sets two methods side by side, the point alone with unblended lines, and the stump-blended manner that takes the higher finish.
6932-pictures-every-child-should-know-a-:
Dolores Bacon gathers the world's art masterpieces for young people, with pictures drawn from great paintings. Her acknowledgments thank writers on artists and pictures, from Sadakichi Hartmann and Muther to Russell Sturgis and Ida Prentice Whitcomb. The introduction traces art from lines cut in clay and hollowed wood, through crude color and drawing, to the Egyptian habit of preserving the fashions of the time.

Man's urge to decorate his belongings, Bacon argues, marks one of the earliest signs of civilization. Each picture in the book is chosen to teach a child to look, and the text explains artist, subject, and craft in plain words. The volume aims to put fine art within reach of young eyes and young minds.
69323-black-nick-the-hermit-of-the-hills:
Black Nick, the Hermit of the Hills, or the Expiated Crime, is a dime novel by Frederick Whittaker. Its subtitle calls it a story of Burgoyne's surrender. Beadle and Adams published it at New York, with copyright entered in eighteen seventy three. Chapter one is called The Wood Fiend. It opens in a lonely forest stretching from the Hudson toward the Mississippi.

Five Indian warriors in full war paint steal into a small clearing, the tale says. They halt by a spring as the sun sets in an angry crimson glow. Their leader scans the ground round the spring with a practiced eye. He has not been here, he remarks. A young brave scorns the pale faces as liars. The leader answers quietly that there are good and bad pale faces alike.
69335-christmas-eve-at-mulligan-s:
Christmas Eve at Mulligan is a Christmas play for schools and churches by Marie Irish, printed at Dayton, Ohio, by the Paine Publishing Company. Irish wrote Choice Christmas Entertainments, The Primary Christmas Book, and Best Christmas Pantomimes. The piece comes with song lists for welcome and closing numbers.

In the talk, Katie scolds Rosie for wanting a doll when dear Dannie is trying to get his eyes well. Katie wants nothing if he can just be made to see, though that takes lots of money. The Mulligan home thus holds a blind boy hope at the heart of its Christmas eve. Songs for teachers programs frame the play, with welcome songs and closing songs named at the front. Groups get a warm, short holiday piece with a tender core.
69367-an-apology-for-abolitionists-addre:
The Anti-Slavery Society of Meriden, Connecticut, issued this apology for abolitionists in 1837, a second edition printed at Middletown. Apology here means defense, not regret. The society tells its fellow citizens that it speaks from a regard for their good opinion, and from love of the cause near its heart.

It lays the opposition to abolition on trade, political, and family ties to slavery, and on plain misunderstanding of the society's aims. It claims the right to publish opinions on the customs of any country, and to call an institution immoral where it finds it so. The pamphlet is a calm, stiff piece of the pamphlet war that preceded the Civil War.
69785-west-lawn-and-the-rector-of-st-mar:
West Lawn, by Mary Holmes, was published at New York in 1874. Carleton issued it, with a second tale bound in. The Rector of St Mark's follows the novel proper. A front list prices fifteen Holmes novels alike. Tempest and Sunshine and Lena Rivers head that list. West Lawn runs to twenty eight chapters. Diaries and letters carry the story. Dora keeps a diary; Dr West keeps one too. Jessie writes hers; Richard tells his own story. An engagement, a shadow of death, and a bridal day fill the middle.

Breaking the engagement and giving in marriage close the plot. The Rector of St Mark's is told by days of the week. Friday afternoon opens it; a trip to Newport ends the part shown. Holmes writes domestic fiction in papers and journals.
6980-tales-of-st-austin-s:
Wodehouse gathers school stories from the Captain and the Public School Magazine in Tales of St Austin's, with one tale printed here for the first time. The preface owns one story as a failure, in Wodehouse's own dry phrase, and dedicates the book to his mother. Contents include How Pillingshot Scored, The Odd Trick, and Uncle John told in letters. Harrison's slight error and Bradshaw's little story follow.

A shocking affair, the babe and the dragon, and the maneuvers of Charteris follow. How Payne Bucked Up, the Tabby Terror, a prize poem, and notes on cricket and the Tom Brown question come after. Pillingshot opens annoyed, disgusted, and mortified at a master's word on his term's work. The tales keep a light schoolboy humor throughout.
70426-men-of-marlowe-s:
Dudeney wrote Men of Marlowe's, a book of linked tales of the men who live in one English inn of court. The tales are so interrelated, a note in the book says, as almost to make a continuous novel. Like the Temple in London, Marlowe's is a place where lawyers and lodgers live side by side, and each man's tale touches the next.

The contents run from The One in Red and Arnold's Laundress to a piece called simply Why. Jimmy, Game Feathers, and Mortgaged follow, with An Interlude and A Political Woman between. Beyond the Gray Gate and The Set at Seven build the circle, and Hopkins closes it. Dudeney was praised in her day for insight into the human heart and for vigor and sanity of mind, and Sussex was her usual ground.
70823-retrospective-exhibition-of-import:
Important Works of John Singer Sargent is a show catalogue of 1924. The Grand Central Art Galleries held the retrospective that winter. It ran from February 23 to March 22. The galleries stood in Grand Central Terminal, on Vanderbilt Avenue. The Painters and Sculptors Gallery Association held the copyright. Juley and Son took the photographs for the book. Trustees and officers head the opening pages. Clark presides; DeForest and Gifford serve under him. Lay members are listed city by city. New York names fill the longest roll. Tiffany, Warburg, and a Vanderbilt stand among them. Chicago, Boston, and Philadelphia add their patrons.

The catalogue records what the galleries gathered for one season. Portraits and figure pieces made Sargent's fame, in oil and charcoal alike. A generation of sitters faces the reader in these plates.
71201-betty-at-st-benedick-s:
Ethel Talbot wrote Betty at St Benedick's, a school story for girls printed in London, Edinburgh, and New York. A front print shows a tumble-down cottage. On the way to school opens the tale. The whole family is at the station to see Betty off: dad, the twins, and the baby. The baby is not to be called baby now, Aunt Frances has ruled.

At St Benedick's come the Daisy mascot, the Guide cup lost and hunted, a fairy piper, and a wood called Witch's Wood. Betty keeps a secret, then shares it, and all comes right. Schoolgirl fans get a warm tale of forms, games, and friendship.
71791-six-little-bunkers-at-farmer-joel-:
Laura Lee Hope wrote Six Little Bunkers at Farmer Joel's for young readers, and Grosset and Dunlap put it out in New York in 1923. Walter Rogers drew the pictures. The six Bunker children leave home for a stay on a farm, where plain country days turn into small trials and treats.

Early chapters put Russ in danger and send the children off in a load of flowers. At the farm they play in the hay and watch the cows come home. Bees, a mad bull, and a honey tree stir up mild alarms. A lost boy, a picnic, an ice cave, and a strawberry shortcake fill the later pages. Hope keeps the tone warm and safe, with each scrape solved by bedtime.
72444-the-crime-at-vanderlynden-s:
R H Mottram wrote a novel published at London in 1926, by the author of The Spanish Farm, which won the Hawthornden Prize for 1924. A song of Kitchener's army heads the title page: oh my, I don't want to die, I want to go home. High up in the pale Flemish sky, the novel opens, aeroplanes wheel and dart like bright insects. Sun glints on metallic bodies and translucent wings.

Below the planes spreads the wartime landscape of Flanders. Mottram served in France and wrote the Spanish Farm trilogy from the ranks. His crime at a Flemish farm mixes murder with the war's long shadow. Chatto and Windus published the novel.
74045-the-lakewood-boys-on-the-lazy-s:
The Lakewood Boys on the Lazy S, by Wyman, is a boys ranch tale of 1925. Wyman was dean of the Pennsylvania Military College when he wrote the series. Burt published the book at New York for readers of twelve to sixteen. A front plate shows a horse turning sharp and all but unseating a boy.

The Lakewood Boys in the Frozen North leads the series list in the front. The Lost Mine, the Polo Ponies, and the South Sea Islands volumes follow there. The Golden Boys series by the same hand stands in his other credits. A western ranch named the Lazy S gives this volume its ground and sport. Schoolboy pals trade the classroom for cattle country in the tale.
74056-life-and-works-of-alexander-csoma-:
Life and Works of Alexander Csoma de Koros is a biography by Theodore Duka. Trubner published it in London in 1885. Its subtitle calls it a biography compiled chiefly from unpublished data. A brief notice of each published work and essay is added. Duka was a retired surgeon major of the Bengal medical service. He was a corresponding member of the Hungarian academy of sciences. A preface admits the authentic data are scanty.

They still form a connected narrative of the chief events, it holds. The subject was a remarkable man of science, the preface says. He never published anything but in the English tongue. Few foreign scholars have been honoured by Englishmen as he was. A memorial over his grave bears testimony to that honour. His best years were offered to British government service. Csoma founded the study of Tibetan in the West.
74942-heimweh-the-siren-the-loaded-gun-l:
John Luther Long gathered these tales in one volume, printed by Macmillan in New York in 1905. Long had written Madame Butterfly, and his fame rode on it. The catalog title is the whole table of contents strung together. A dedication hopes the stories serve readers sick with longing, whether for squalid homes on earth or mansions above.

Heimweh, homesickness, leads the book in eleven short chapters. The Siren dives to the bottom of the sea. The Loaded Gun turns on three gentlemen of Philadelphia and a fool and his money. Liebereich builds the house that he and Emmy built. Iupiter Tonans and Sis follow, with Thor's Emerald and Guile to close. Long writes in brief, intense scenes, mixing German song, American streets, and the sea. The collection is his miscellany of longing.
76344-over-bemerton-s:
Over Bemerton's, published in 1908, is Lucas's easy-going chronicle of a Westminster lodging and its circle. The narrator returns from travel and finds a home in Westminster, near Queen Anne's Gate. Bemerton, his landlord, gives him the freedom of a treasury of books. Bed books from that hoard open two stretches of the tale.

Around the house gather the Wynnes, the Duckies and Dabney of The Balance. A county cricketer, a suffragette and an heir of the ages pass through. The narrator tries second-hand bookselling, lends money and assists at two weddings. He is whirled away by the 2.20 train from Charing Cross to meet the queen of the Adriatic. The link, he finds, is how surely people sway each other.
78889-observations-on-the-geology-zoolog:
Robert Bell, a geologist with the Geological and Natural History Survey of Canada, reported here on Hudson Strait and Hudson Bay. His party sailed on the government steamship Alert in 1885, the second such trip. The report was printed at Montreal in 1885 by authority of Parliament, and Bell sent it to the survey's director that spring.

Bell acted as both geologist and naturalist for the voyage. His pages record the rocks of the strait and bay, the animals found there, and the plants that grow in that cold region. A first report in December 1885 had sketched the field work; this volume gives the fuller account. It stands as an early scientific survey of Canada's northern waters.
8093-the-canadian-elocutionist-designed-:
Anna K. Howard, LL. B. , also known as Anna Halleck Kelsey, teacher of elocution and English literature, wrote this Canadian elocutionist for colleges, schools, and self-instruction. It pairs principles, rules, illustrations, and exercises for speaking well with a copious selection, in prose and poetry, of pieces adapted for reading, recitation, and practice. Its motto, from Chesterfield, holds that the manner of speaking matters as much as the matter.

Howard's aim was practical: to give teachers and students a single convenient book for lessons in voice, gesture, and delivery. The anthology ranges widely, so practice never grows stale. As a record of how a century ago students learned to stand and speak, the book is both a teaching manual and a charming period piece.
a-book-of-the-play-studies-and-illustrat: Dutton Cook writes a study of the theatre for playgoers and lovers of the stage. Its chapters treat playgoers, the master of the revels, the licenser, the examiner of plays, and strolling players. Cook draws on stage history and anecdote to show how plays were made, licensed, and received. The book aims to serve and entertain all who care for the life of the theatre.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Theodore Roosevelt's supplemental messages and papers fill this volume of the presidential compilation. Born in New York in 1858, Roosevelt rose from assemblyman to president, and the volume records his official words. It belongs to a series that prints each president's messages for the public record. Readers find here the formal voice of Roosevelt's presidency.
a-gentleman-of-france-being-the-memoirs-:
Stanley John Weyman tells his romance as the memoirs of Gaston de Bonne, Sieur de Marsac, a poor gentleman of France who takes service with Henry of Navarre. The long contents list promises fights on stairs, royal peril, pestilence and famine, and the death of a king. Marsac begins as a nobody with a sword and a name.

Across thirty-six chapters he rides through the French wars of religion, meets Rosny and Mademoiselle de la Vire, and faces the League's offers and threats. Weyman grounds the duels and escapes in real events of Henry IV's struggle for his throne. The first-person voice gives the adventure a modest, soldierly charm.
a-little-dinner-at-timmins-s:
William Makepeace Thackeray introduces Mr. and Mrs. Fitzroy Timmins of Lilliput Street, a neat street near the Park, and relations, distantly, of the Earl of Bungay. Timmins is a barrister on the Northern Circuit. A sudden piece of luck, papers in a railway case sent by great solicitors, goes to his head at once.

He buys looking-glasses for his small drawing rooms and resolves to give a dinner beyond his means. Thackeray follows the invitations, the borrowed plate, the guests' snobbery, and the bill, with the delight of a man who knew every rung of London's social ladder. The sketch is a small, perfect satire of keeping up appearances.
a-residence-in-france-with-an-excursion-: James Fenimore Cooper recounts living in France, travelling up the Rhine, and visiting Switzerland a second time, first reached in 1828 and revisited in 1832. The preface warns of a long digression touching another country, matter not strictly tied to the principal subject, which the author embraces for its own interest. Four years left the sublime nature of Switzerland unchanged, he writes, while its political and social surface had seriously altered.
a-short-life-of-abraham-lincoln-condense: John George Nicolay condenses a short life of Abraham Lincoln from Nicolay and Hay's larger history, published in 1904. The contents open with ancestry, Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks, Rock Spring Farm, Lincoln's birth, Kentucky schools, and the journey to Indiana. Pigeon Creek, Gentryville, work and books, a flatboat voyage to New Orleans, and the journey to Illinois follow, carrying the future president from frontier boyhood toward public life.
bowdoin-boys-in-labrador-an-account-of-t:
Jonathan Prince Cilley Jr wrote Bowdoin Boys in Labrador, printed by the Rockland Publishing Company of Maine. Cilley tells of the Bowdoin College expedition to Labrador led by Professor Leslie A Lee of the biological department. The schooner Julia A Decker carries the party north in 1891.

Fog at the Gut of Canso opens the tale, with Lee measuring Micmac men, women, and children for science. The voyage then works up the Labrador coast among birds, fish, and Moravian mission folk. Puffins crowd the cliffs so thick that shooting turns to slaughter in the boys' own words. Letters from mission wives close the set. Students read a real college field trip: part log, part science, part travel tale.
britannica-1911-almack-s:
Balls made Almack's famous. In 1765 William Almack built assembly rooms in King's Street, St James's, where ten guineas bought twelve weeks of weekly balls. A committee of ladies of rank ruled admission, and getting in was exceedingly hard. Almack, by the way, is usually said to be an anagram of Macall or McCaul, the founder's real name.

A year before the rooms, in 1764, he had opened a gentlemen's club in Pall Mall, famed for high-stakes play. That club later passed to Brooks and lives on as Brooks's Club in St James's Street. Almack died in 1781; his niece took over the rooms, which ran as Willis's Rooms until 1890. A new London social club brought the Almack's name back in 1904.
britannica-1911-tattersall-s:
Tattersall's, the London horse auction mart, was founded in seventeen sixty six, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its founder was Richard Tattersall, who had been stud groom to the Duke of Kingston. The first site stood near Hyde Park Corner, then on the edge of London.

Two rooms were set aside for Jockey Club members. They became a meeting place for sporting and betting men. Great stud sales were held there, for the Duke of Kingston and for the Prince of Wales. The prince was a friend of the founder and shared a newspaper venture with him. Son and grandson in turn ran the firm and spread its work to France. A later head moved the mart to Knightsbridge when the long lease ran out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-george-:
Saint George's is the Newfoundland diocese taking in the western south coast and the Gulf of Saint Lawrence shore nearly to the Strait of Belle Isle. For years it was little more than the historic French shore. Anglo-French treaties discouraged permanent settlement there, yet the rich herring fishery drew adventurers anyway, and about 2000 people had built log cabins in its sheltered bays by 1850. Until that year no resident Catholic priest served the coast, apart from rare visits by a French warship's chaplain.

The first resident priest, Alexandre Belanger, arrived on 7 September 1850, and Thomas Sears of Antigonish followed on 2 November 1868 as the coast's true apostle and social reformer. He won a mail steamer in 1872 and saw magistracy and police established in 1878. The territory became a prefecture in 1870, with Sears as prefect in 1871, and it was raised to a vicariate in 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abbey-of-:
The Abbey of Bury St Edmund's began with Sigebert, King of the East Angles, who resigned his crown for a monastery about 537. It grew celebrated when King Edmund's relics arrived in 903, and the town, till then Boedericsworth, became St Edmund's Bury. Under Canute, Benedictines replaced secular canons. In 1095 the relics moved to Abbot Baldwin's church. The shrine grew in fame and wealth until the monastery ranked second to Glastonbury, but a 1465 fire caused irreparable loss.

The abbot sat in Parliament with jurisdiction over town and neighbourhood. Eighty monks could be housed, but over two hundred lived in the abbey. At the dissolution revenues stood at £2,366, worth over £20,000 in present money. In the abbey church in 1214 Cardinal Langton read the Charter of Liberties at the high altar, later signed as Magna Charta by John. Henry VIII dissolved the abbey in 1539, leaving gateway, bridge, and ruins, with the relics' fate undecided.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1660-n-s:
The first full year of Samuel Pepys's Diary is gathered in this Complete 1660 volume, New Series, running from the manuscript's opening on January 1st. The Commonwealth dies in these pages: Monk's march, Montagu's fleet, and the King's return in May pass before a young clerk's shorthand. Pepys rises with his patron Sandwich into the Navy Office. He ends the year with a house, a salary, and a diary habit that would last nine more years.

Day by day, the year mixes great events with dinners, music, quarrels with his wife Elizabeth, and the price of everything. Pepys writes his famous new-year resolutions and breaks them on schedule. The shorthand was never meant for readers, which is why readers trust it. Anyone sampling the Diary whole should begin with 1660: it is the year Pepys becomes Pepys, and England becomes the Restoration, in the same handwriting.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1661-n-s:
Samuel Pepys's second full year is gathered in this Complete 1661 volume, New Series, the Diary from January to December of the coronation year. Pepys is now Clerk of the Acts at the Navy Office, a householder in Seething Lane, and a man keeping shorthand notes on his own rise. Charles II is crowned in April with Pepys in the Abbey crowd. The death of his uncle Robert sets a Brampton inheritance in motion, and the diarist rides down to settle it.

Theatre first nights, tavern music, his wife Elizabeth's lessons, and office feuds with Batten and Penn fill the ordinary weeks. Pepys records his ambition as frankly as his dinners, and judges both. Readers taking the year whole watch the Diary find its subject. It is not great events. It is a young official's daily making of himself, with the court glittering at his page's edge.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1662-n-s:
The year 1662 stands complete in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary, the spring of the Queen's arrival and the autumn of Dunkirk's sale. Pepys spends the year rising in plain sight. He inspects Portsmouth with Carteret and Penn. He sits with the Navy Board at St. James's under the Duke's own eye. The Queen lands and marries in May, and the diarist's fleet does the fetching and the fireworks. At home his Seething Lane house fills with pictures, hangings, and his wife's music lessons.

No disaster marks this year, which is its value. The Diary shows ordinary excellence instead: accounts kept, ships surveyed, dinners scored, ambitions confessed. Pepys is twenty-nine and worth watching precisely because nothing forces him to be interesting. Readers taking 1662 whole get the baseline of the Restoration world, the year against which plague, fire, and war will later be measured in the same shorthand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1663-n-s:
The year 1663 stands complete in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary, the diarist's fourth year of shorthand. Pepys is thirty and settled. He is Clerk of the Acts, a Trinity House brother, and a man whose credit rises at Court and on the Exchange. The year's entries run from Brampton estate settlements to Navy Office sittings. His father and Uncle Thomas fill the family pages. His wife Elizabeth presides over a house that grows finer by the season.

War talk shadows the summer, moving toward the war of 1665. Pepys audits ships and stores like a man who expects to be believed later. At home there is music, good wine, and Mrs. Lane at Westminster. Readers taking 1663 whole get the Diary at cruising speed. No plague, no fire, not yet. Just a capable man enjoying his rise, and writing it all down.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1664-n-s:
The year 1664 stands complete in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary. It is the last quiet year before plague and fire remake London. Pepys spends it becoming indispensable. He serves the Navy Board and the Tangier committee. In June his surgeon warns him the stone may have returned, and the fear rides under the summer's work. By autumn the navy is fitting in earnest for the Dutch war that everyone expects and no one has declared.

At home the year is music, dinners, and his wife's painting and dancing masters. His shorthand catches his vanities as faithfully as his audits. Readers taking 1664 whole get the Diary at full strength. The great public disasters are still offstage.
