What fills the page is competence: one man's, growing daily, in a city that will soon need all of it.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1665-n-s:
Samuel Pepys's plague year is gathered whole in this New Series volume, the Diary of 1665 from January to December. It begins with expense accounts and a fellowship of the Royal Society. It darkens by the month. War is declared in March. The fleet wins at Lowestoft in June while crosses appear on London doors. Pepys sends his wife out of the city and keeps his post at Greenwich, and walks streets where the weekly dead climb past seven thousand in September.

The year's second half is the wonder: business, dinners, and a wedding party carried on over the pits. Pepys buries nothing but his fears in these pages. He records them, prices them, and goes to the office. Readers taking 1665 whole get the century's most studied year through its most honest eyes. It is the year a clerk proved that daily paperwork is also a form of courage.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1666-n-s:
All of 1666, the Fire year, is gathered in this New Series volume of Pepys's Diary. It opens in January with the diarist dictating his pursers' report before dawn. It climbs through the Four Days' Battle in June, fought within hearing of the coast. August finds Pepys worth fifty-seven hundred pounds, the richest of his life. September burns his city down. He rows the King his famous advice, pulls down houses, and buries his wine and cheese in a pit.

The rest of the year is ashes and creditors: a broke navy and a fenced ruin. Pepys works through all of it, and ends the year necessary. Readers taking 1666 whole get the most dramatic twelve months of the Diary in one binding. No novelist would dare stack plague's aftermath, a naval war, and the Great Fire into a single clerk's year.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1667-n-s:
The whole of 1667, Pepys's year of ice and defeat, is gathered in this New Series volume of the Diary. It opens in hard frost, the Thames frozen, the diarist doubting England can float a fleet. Spring proves the doubt: thirty thousand pounds against ten times the need. June brings the Dutch into the Medway, the chain broken, the Royal Charles towed away, and Pepys sending his family and his gold out of a city he expects to be sacked. No Englishman wrote a better account of his country's worst week.

Peace at Breda ends the war in July. The year closes in inquiries and generals assigning blame. Pepys ends it with his papers in order and his credit, almost alone among navy men, intact. Readers taking 1667 whole get the Diary's darkest arc after the Fire, and its author at his most valuable: the clerk who warned everyone, in writing, beforehand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1668-n-s:
Samuel Pepys's ninth year of shorthand fills this New Series volume, the Diary of 1668 whole. It is the year of the tickets defence, when Pepys and Coventry rehearsed their case before the Commons like actors. It is also the year of Deb Willet. The maid who brushed his hair in April is embraced in October, discovered by his wife, and dismissed in tears. Pepys's entries swing between Parliament and the bedroom with the same unflinching pen, recording his defence, his desire, and his remorse.

Under both stories runs a third: his eyes. By lamplight the page hurts. His wife and his boy read aloud to him in the evenings, Wilkins's new Real Character among the books. Readers taking 1668 whole get the Diary in late flower, richer and sadder than the early years. The clerk has become a personage. The cost, itemized nightly, is the sight he is spending to write.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-complete-1669-n-s:
The Diary's last year is gathered in this New Series volume, Samuel Pepys's record for 1669, ending on the final day of May. Winter brings a silver warming-pan he doubts he should accept, and a walnut cabinet, eleven pounds, bought for his wife's New Year gift. Spring brings a court-martial where Pepys watches commanders conspire to ruin a purser. His public work is as sharp as ever. It is the private act of writing that is failing, page by page, with his eyes.

On May 31st he closes the journal he believes is costing him his sight. The last entries are calm: dinner, his wife, and bed. Readers taking 1669 whole get five months only, and an ending no editor would dare invent. The greatest diary in English stops not with an event but with a pair of tired eyes.
doe-osti-17047517-moving-beyond-the-mini:
Slide deck by Sherin Ann Abraham, dated July 2026, presents October 2025 results on a grid screening rule that may now block more good projects than it protects. The minimum daytime load screen is a quick check used when rooftop solar and other local generators seek to connect to a feeder. Failing the screen forces a slow, detailed study.

The screen began in the early 2000s as a cautious rule of thumb, tied to a 15 percent penetration limit. The deck argues it is now too strict, since certified smart inverters greatly cut islanding risk. Model based checks on heat, voltage, and protection could replace it, speeding connections and clearing backlogs safely.
doe-osti-2583487-electric-vehicle-supply:
Site assessment NREL/TP-5400-92115, by Dana Truffer-Moudra, Eliseo Esparza, and Cabell Hodge, plans electric vehicle charging for the Army Corps of Engineers' Chena site near Fairbanks, Alaska. Few places punish EVs like interior Alaska. The report opens with the weather itself, including the cold snap of January 21 to February 4, 2024, then inventories the site's small fleet and its electrical capacity.

Cold changes the charging math. A plugged-in vehicle can pull current to warm its battery, which prolongs battery life, so the assessment recommends one charger per vehicle rather than sharing. Three pedestal-mounted Level 2 chargers are specified for the three site vehicles, costed in both 50-amp and 80-amp versions. Design guidelines cover pedestal equipment, networked charging, and usage reporting. The result is a buildable plan for fleet electrification where temperatures do not merely inconvenience batteries but threaten them.
doe-osti-2583685-improved-weld-residual-:
Argonne report ANL-25/23, by Cheng-Hau Yang, Mark C. Messner, and Tianchen Hu, improves BlackBear, the lab's MOOSE-based code for simulating welding. Welds lock in stress as they cool, and predicting that stress decides whether a part cracks years later. BlackBear models the heat and force process, but ease of use and solver strength needed work. The report pursues both.

For users, a central default block rule makes coverage checks run the same way across objects. A new modular action folds moving heat source setup into one configuration. It handles path parsing, subdomain changes, and kernel rules together. For the solver, a new way of seeding initial values on the growing domain improves convergence as material is added. Tests include heat flow with staged material addition and elasticity with time-based deposition. Two- and three-dimensional welding simulations close the checks, including a slot weld study.
doe-osti-2589200-membrane-based-ionic-li:
Saeed Moghaddam of the University of Florida and Paul Glanville of GTI Energy led this technical progress report for award DE-EE0009162, covering April 2020 through March 2025 and dated July 30, 2025. The system under development moves dehumidification and heating onto a membrane-based ionic liquid absorption cycle, aiming at efficiency conventional vapor compression cannot reach.

Ionic liquids drink water vapor from air without evaporating refrigerant, and membranes keep the liquid where it belongs. The engineering is a chain of trade-offs. One limit traced through the report is thermal: the heat exchanger surface must stay at or below 190 degrees Celsius to avoid degrading the ionic liquid. Temperature maps of the exchanger surface, against flue gases inside, show the hot spots the design must tame. Progress reports like this one document the build-measure-fix loop in detail, component by component, on the way to a working ultra-efficient system.
doe-osti-2589340-innovative-joints-for-h: Brookhaven National Laboratory's final filing for CRADA C-21-04 with Renaissance Americas Inc. is a short closeout record, not a research report. The project, led at Brookhaven by Ramesh Gupta, was meant to develop better joints for high-temperature superconducting tapes. Work ended early when the company changed its business plans. Brookhaven's part never went past meetings and early checks, and no test results or outcomes were reached.
doe-osti-2997595-tank-48h-phase-1-initia:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2025-00506, by Elizabeth Craig, dated September 2025, characterizes a radioactive waste sample before a chemistry test. Tank 48H at the Savannah River Site holds waste rich in tetraphenylborate, a compound slated for destruction with sodium permanganate. Sample HTF-48-25-17 was drawn on 25 February 2025 and studied in the laboratory's shielded cells as phase one of a multi-phase test plan.

The slurry's average density was 1.28 grams per milliliter, with total dried solids at 27.4 percent by weight. Cesium-137 measured 2.13 times ten to the seventh disintegrations per minute per milliliter in the liquid part. Chromatography found tetraphenylborate at 18,200 milligrams per liter in the slurry, plus phenol and biphenyl. Toluene was the only volatile organic detected, at 7.75 milligrams per liter. Later test phases dose this same waste with permanganate against this baseline.
doe-osti-2998225-effects-of-borate-and-o:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-25-30019, by Ceren Kutahyali Aslani, issued 8 October 2025, measures how waste chemicals change uranium solubility in repository brine. The setting is the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant, where brine could one day reach buried waste. Borate in the brine and organic chemicals from the waste itself, acetate, oxalate, citrate, and EDTA, can each pull uranium into solution.

Expected organic levels were computed from the project inventory against a minimum brine volume of 17,400 cubic meters. Experiments used brines at 90 percent of the reference strength. Earlier work cited shows borate raising uranium solubility in salt solutions at total boron above 0.04 molar across the near-neutral to mildly alkaline range, likely through uranium-borate complexes in the water. Solubility numbers from this study feed the repository's safety calculations.
doe-osti-2998774-tank-48h-phase-1-initia:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2025-00583, by Elizabeth Craig, Corey Martin, Matthew Siegfried and Nicholas Wilson, dated October 2025, covers first-phase tests on waste tank 48H. The tank holds about 270,000 gallons of legacy material, including roughly 20,000 kilograms of tetraphenylborate solids left from an old treatment process. That organic material must be broken down before the tank can return to normal service.

Tests used a non-radioactive copy of the tank slurry and sodium permanganate, a strong oxidiser, to attack the tetraphenylborate. Seven runs sat in 250-millilitre flasks in a shaker oven for 56 days at pH 14. Two more ran in 2-litre jacketed vessels with live off-gas monitoring. Breakdown rose with time, heat and dose. Several smaller doses beat one equal total dose, and a triple dose totalling 4.5 parts matched a single 9-part dose.
doe-osti-3002002-participation-in-and-as:
A seven-author Oak Ridge team led by Alex Shaw reports on a public workshop in ORNL/TM-2025/4278, dated October 2025. The workshop was the second held by the DNCSH project, a joint Energy Department and Nuclear Regulatory Commission effort on criticality safety. DNCSH covers commercial-scale fuel cycles and transport for HALEU, uranium enriched beyond standard reactor fuel. The project began under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.

The report covers who attended, what a pre-workshop survey found, and what the sessions covered. Discussion centered on gaps in the experiment data used to check criticality safety calculations. An appendix weighs fuel options, from uranium-zirconium metal to molten salt fuels, with near-term and long-term priorities. Regulators and fuel firms use such workshops to agree on what data must come next.
doe-osti-3002705-in-conduit-hydropower-f:
Scott DeNeale, Lindsay Ashworth, Antonia Chu, Lora Davis, and Jeremy Wells examine a niche power source in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2024/3739, dated October 2025. In-conduit hydropower places small turbines inside public water supply pipes, harvesting energy from pressure and flow that utilities must manage anyway. No new dam is needed, which is the idea's main appeal.

The report focuses on why projects stall and what they cost. Chapters weigh turbine choices, including pumps run in reverse as turbines, against utility rules and water quality duties. Construction cost trends from the Bureau of Reclamation inform the estimates. The audience is water utilities and developers weighing a first installation. The authors give them the development hurdles plainly, so a promising site is not mistaken for an easy one.
doe-osti-3003151-resolving-issues-regard:
Nicholas Alexander Smith of Los Alamos, Shiloh Elliott of Sandia, and Christopher Gazze, Robert Marek, and Jessica White-Horton, with Murray Smith, study a disposal dilemma in report LA-UR-25-31206, issued November 13, 2025. Some nuclear waste still carries safeguards obligations: inspectors must account for its material even after burial. The report explores disposal concepts for such material in near-surface and intermediate-depth sites.

Two case studies structure the work, prepared for an Energy Department safeguards office. Each traces the safeguards challenges of its scenario and the possible fixes. A glossary and an expert team roster support the analysis. The underlying tension is plain: disposal aims to close the books on waste forever, while safeguards aim to keep verifying it. The concepts here try to satisfy both duties at once.
doe-osti-3004708-characterization-of-gas:
R. S. Augusto and E. Skordis characterize a radiation source in Brookhaven technical note BNL-229167-2025-TECH, dated November 2025. The source is gas bremsstrahlung: X-rays spat out when electrons in a storage ring graze residual gas molecules. At the Electron-Ion Collider, the electron ring is large and powerful, so even this faint source can dose components over years of running.

The team used the FLUKA Monte Carlo transport code, in its 2025.1 and 4-5.1 versions, to build credible source terms for the ring's arc cells. Synchrotron radiation studies from the same group provide the comparison background. The collider will collide polarized electrons and ions at 20 to 140 GeV per nucleon. Machine protection staff use source characterizations like this one when they place shielding and set component lifetimes.
doe-osti-3008386-elm-1016706669-aa-b581-: Only pages 4 and 5 of a generator load analysis survive in LLNL-TR-2014201, a Lawrence Livermore summary by Adam Heal. The pages cover building B581 equipment GDE01. Its nameplate reads 150 kilowatts, but the standby load measured on December 12, 2024 was 81 kilowatts. That is 54 percent of rating, inside the recommended 40 to 70 percent loading band. The pages also flag harmonic distortion from nonlinear loads that has upset NIF UPS units tied to the set.
doe-osti-3013190-carbon-capture-pilot-at:
TDA Research's final technical report for award DE-CD0000054, led by Gokhan Alptekin, covers a carbon capture pilot planned for the Dry Fork Power Station in Gillette, Wyoming. The pilot would run at the Wyoming Integrated Test Center beside the coal plant. TDA's system uses a solid physical adsorbent in a vacuum and concentration swing process to strip carbon dioxide from flue gas holding about 13 percent CO2 by volume.

The plan was phased: design, approvals, construction, then a one-year operating demonstration. DOE terminated the project midway through Phase 1, and this report records progress to that point, with milestone tables split between accepted deliverables and those awaiting feedback. The design targets were capture above 90 percent of emissions at threshold, 95 percent as the objective, with product purity above 95 percent.
doe-osti-3015309-engineering-scale-test-:
A water-lean solvent for post-combustion carbon capture gets an engineering-scale test in an EPRI final report under award DE-FE0031945, dated January 29, 2026. The solvent, EEMPA, was developed at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and targets specific reboiler duties below 2.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide at 12 volume percent inlet concentration, working at under 10 weight percent water with no diluent. Joseph Swisher was principal investigator.

The campaign ran on the Pilot Solvent Test Unit at the National Carbon Capture Center. Its objectives were capture rates of at least 90 percent on both coal-relevant high-concentration gas and gas-turbine-relevant low-concentration gas, with at least two months of testing on each. Sequential design of experiments structured the runs, and emissions and solvent health were tracked through the campaign.
doe-osti-3015901-analysis-of-molten-salt:
Julian D Osorio of the National Laboratory of the Rockies and nine co-authors from Solar Dynamics, Latin American firms and universities, and Colorado School of Mines wrote this January 2026 report, NLR/TP-5500-98065. Mark Mehos and Luca Imponenti are the next names on the byline. The subject is the hot salt tanks that store heat in concentrating solar power plants.

Such tanks let solar plants keep generating after sunset, but central receiver plants running up to 565 degrees Celsius have seen several costly tank failures. The report works on tank sizing and on preheating, the slow warm-up before hot salt first fills a tank. Computer stress models track floor welds and distortion in a tank 24 meters across. Engineers designing the next tanks get sizing and warm-up guidance aimed at the failure modes that hurt earlier plants.
doe-osti-3016983-tasti-grid-a-holistic-v:
Hillary Fishler and Supriya Chinthavali of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote TASTI-GRID, report ORNL/TM-2026/4403, a short study of Florida's electric grid resilience. In December 2025 the American Society of Civil Engineers raised Florida's infrastructure grade to a C+. Even so, extreme weather, aging assets, and fast population growth keep straining the grid.

The study ranks Florida against other states: 46th in impact level during extreme events, 43rd in recovery duration, but 10th in per-minute recovery rate. Outage figures underline the spread: customers averaged 1,488.2 minutes of interruption in major event years, against 66.2 minutes excluding major events. County-level outage cost estimates capture both business and household losses. State planners get a compact, numbers-first case for where resilience money should go first.
doe-osti-3017152-solar-and-storage-integ:
Brian Sergi, Jennie Jorgenson, and Lawryn Kiboma of the national laboratories, with Zack Jensen, Dev Millstein, Natalie Mims Frick, and Fritz Kahrl, presented these slides on June 25, 2025. The project studies solar and storage growth in the United States Southeast. Its core question is resource adequacy: will the grid still have enough capacity at all times as weather-dependent power grows?

The work runs in three phases, covering integration effects, solar forecasting and storage operation, and resource adequacy in energy-limited systems. Modeling used the ReEDS capacity model with representative days drawn from a 2012 weather profile. Capacity credit and stress period work relied on seven years of hourly data, from 2007 to 2013 by default. The team stresses the study is research, not a policy recommendation. Grid planners still get a sharper method for valuing solar and storage.
doe-osti-3017709-gallium-arsenide-semico:
Caitlin Chapin of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this February 2026 report, LLNL-TR-2014850, on gallium arsenide semiconductor opening switches. Project 23-ERD-031 studied switches in both silicon and gallium arsenide. An opening switch holds off high voltage, then snaps open in nanoseconds to release a pulse. Such switches are critical parts for pulsed power systems.

Applications named in the report include directed energy systems and dielectric wall accelerators. A dielectric wall accelerator is a compact accelerator concept with uses in radiation therapy as well as strategic deterrence. Under this funding the team developed silicon switch designs that suppress an unwanted precursor effect in the pulse. Pulsers built from these devices have also spun off further work. The report frames the switch as a key enabling technology: small component, system-level consequences for any machine that lives on fast, high-power pulses.
doe-osti-3018062-tcf-base-technology-spe:
Arun Persaud of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory led this Technology Commercialization Fund final report, dated January 30, 2026, on a real-time soil core scanner. Project TC-23LB020202 ran from October 2023 to December 2025, with Adelphi Technology as partner. The scanner measures carbon and other elements in soil cores on the spot, using neutron methods Persaud's group also applies in nuclear physics.

Knowing soil carbon quickly and cheaply matters for carbon accounting: digging, shipping, and lab drying is slow and expensive. Federal funding came to 839,956 dollars against 840,000 planned, with 360,000 dollars of cost share. The report lists the technical publications the project produced. It also notes the methods are helping planetary research through a new NASA grant. The document is a commercialization close-out: what was built, what it cost, and where the technique goes next.
doe-osti-3020304-integrated-energy-water:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory white paper PNNL-38617, by Abigayle Hodson and four co-authors, argues that the United States cannot manage water and energy risks with the data it currently collects. The two systems depend on each other, yet they are managed and measured separately. When power fails, water and wastewater service can fail in cascade, and planners lack standardized numbers to see it coming.

The paper notes that the energy sector has the Energy Information Administration's standardized datasets, while water has nothing comparable across its 148,000 public water systems and 15,000 wastewater plants. It calls for an integrated, empirical data foundation to support regional management, benchmarking, and efficiency research. Such data would also feed the National Risk Register and planning for a proposed emergency support function for water.
doe-osti-3020546-diesel-fuel-consumption:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report LBNL-2001717, by Carolyn Szum and Hanna Breunig, tackles a basic data gap: nobody directly reports how much diesel fuel each United States open-pit mine burns. Mines publish production figures, ore grades, and capacities, but not fuel use. The authors built a transparent framework to estimate site-level diesel consumption and prices when direct reporting is missing, with a structured confidence rating for each method.

They demonstrated the framework on 21 prominent open-pit mines, converting reported activity data into diesel estimates and mapping the geographic spread of consumption. The findings support supply chain analysis for the United States industrial base and better transparency in mining-sector energy use. The authors plan dataset updates and method validation so the estimates stay useful as mine reporting changes.
doe-osti-3020632-advanced-conductor-test:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-90228, by Crash Bell, Steven Cook, Jake Gentle, Abby Neumann, and Nikki Rasmussen, reports fire testing of Southwire's 995.0 kcmil ACCS/TW/C7 advanced conductor. Its composite core is meant to carry heavy loads with less sag than steel-reinforced designs, a route to more transmission capacity on existing corridors. The laboratory's Advanced Grid Solutions team examined how the conductor behaves when wildfire heat reaches it.

The report walks through specimen preparation in detail: uncoiling, brooming out the strands, cutting and cleaning the composite core, and potting the ends in epoxy so tensile loads grip evenly. Samples then faced flame exposure in the fire chamber, followed by rated breaking strength testing to compare post-fire strength with specifications. Cleaning proved crucial, since leftover residue could weaken the epoxy bond and distort results.
doe-osti-3021994-integrated-multi-fideli:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38154, by Wei Du and eight co-authors, dated August 2025, presents DistribuDyn, a platform for watching distribution grids move, not just settle. Planning tools usually study steady states, but feeders crowded with inverter-based solar, batteries, and variable loads behave dynamically during faults and switching. Commercial tools offer limited ability to simulate those transients, so the team built a multi-fidelity co-simulation platform.

GridLAB-D, DOE's open-source distribution simulator, gained a network solver able to run short-circuit fault studies. Through the HELICS co-simulation engine, it links with the PSCAD electromagnetic transient tool, so manufacturers' black-box inverter models can run inside realistic feeder models. Machine learning produced white-, gray-, and black-box models of grid-forming and grid-following inverters, validated against field measurements. Frequency events were among the test cases.
doe-osti-3024212-ev-stock-and-load-forec:
Arthur Yip, Cemal Akcicek, Fan Yang, and Paige Jadun presented these slides on October 23, 2025, to the Hawaiian Electric Company's integrated grid planning stakeholder working group. The subject is forecasting how many electric vehicles Hawaii will have, and what load their charging will add. The National Laboratory of the Rockies team used TEMPO, a national transportation demand model that blends energy-economic and travel demand methods.

Slides note that by 2025, projections and ambitions for electric vehicle adoption had risen substantially compared with the previous five years. The method adds Hawaii-specific factors and scenario design on top of the national model. For each scenario, island, and year, outputs include electric vehicle sales share, household and freight vehicle stock, charging availability, and time-resolved charging load profiles that planners can feed into grid studies.
doe-osti-3025680-a-multigigabit-link-lay:
Paul Bachek of Brookhaven National Laboratory's Collider Accelerator Department describes a data link protocol in technical note BNL-229597-2026-TECH, dated March 2026. The protocol runs on AMD UltraScale+ GTH and GTY transceivers and chases an exacting target named in the title: latency that is not just low but deterministic to a single picosecond. Accelerator timing systems live or die on that repeatability.

Implementation details fill the note. Channels are synchronized to one reference clock domain. A transmit or receive clock can be delayed by inverting it or by adding a fixed phase offset through a PLL or MMCM block. With the transceiver in buffer bypass mode, a dual-clock FIFO in the FPGA fabric crosses clock domains and serves as the elastic buffer. The note says the vendor's recommended receiver setup does not cover this case.
doe-osti-3027526-dose-measurement-and-mo:
Joao de Carvalho Saraiva of Brookhaven National Laboratory pairs dose measurements with Monte Carlo simulation for the front end and first optical enclosure of the 27-ID HEX beamline at NSLS-II. The note is BNL-229614-2026-TECH, dated March 2026. Radiation safety around a bright synchrotron beamline rests on knowing the dose field before people work near it. The HEX beamline's source is a triple superconducting wiggler making photons up to several hundred keV.

Calculations used the FLUKA transport code, with the source term computed by the STAC8 program for a 3 GeV primary electron beam at 500 milliamps of stored current. The wiggler's photon spectrum, plotted in photons per second per bandwidth slice, feeds those runs. Measurement and simulation are reported together so each can check the other, the standard pattern for shielding verification work.
doe-osti-3027597-monolithic-encapsulatio:
Nicolas Gaillard of the University of Hawaii reports award DE-EE0010241, which ran September 2022 to March 2024 on a budget of 375,030 dollars, submitted May 5, 2025. Perovskite solar cells are efficient but fragile; moisture creeps in and kills them. The project wrapped the cells in a monolithic encapsulation built from transparent conductive composites, so the protective layer doubles as part of the electrical contact.

Barrier performance is reported as water vapor transmission rates. A plain Aluzine laminate let through 1.48 grams per square meter per day at 25 degrees and full humidity. The multilayer stack of indium zinc oxide, silver, indium zinc oxide, and Aluzine cut that to about 0.088 at 45 percent humidity and 0.084 at 90 percent. The report also notes that thicker inorganic films were found counterproductive in this evaluation.
doe-osti-3028185-wyoming-carbon-blueprin:
Lydia Bailey, Maitri Vijay Dalal, Juan Carlos Duque, and fourteen colleagues, mostly at Los Alamos National Laboratory, wrote the Wyoming Carbon Blueprint, LA-UR-26-22737, issued April 6, 2026. Wyoming holds energy-scale carbon dioxide sources and deep geology suited to storage. The blueprint is a roadmap for joining the two statewide: where capture and storage could go, in what order, and under what rules.

Project-facing chapters read like an application manual. Developers must define an area of interest where environmental, economic, and social impacts will land, and show the project has planned for community health, safety, and welfare. Construction schedules, milestones, workforce estimates, job types, expected in-migration, wage levels, and benefits all belong in the filing. At several hundred pages, the blueprint doubles as the state's reference shelf for carbon management.
doe-osti-3362765-psh-assessment-and-site:
Evan Rosenlieb of the National Laboratory of the Rockies presents these screening slides on pumped storage hydropower for the Chemehuevi Reservation. Pumped storage is a giant water battery: pump water uphill when power is cheap, let it fall back through turbines when power is dear. The lab geospatial and cost models hunt for workable pairs of reservoirs, both open-loop sites tied to existing water and closed-loop pairs built from scratch.

Two gauges rule the screen. Head, the height gap between reservoirs, scores from not feasible under 60 meters to excellent above 400. The length-to-head ratio should sit between 4 and 8 for an ideal site. On the reservation, planned water sites sit flat, far from the high ground. So the verdict is mixed. Big capacity is possible using Lake Havasu. But it needs an upper reservoir in a planned nature area.
doe-osti-3363647-historic-colonial-theat:
Brenna Nicely of the Bethlehem Redevelopment Association reports on a clean energy upgrade at the historic Colonial Theatre in Bethlehem, New Hampshire (award DE-EE0010789, April 2024 to February 2026). The project paired roof renewal with a rooftop solar array on the landmark building.

A new rubber roof with standing seam steel on the main surface was completed in July 2024. Grid interconnection and net metering approvals followed, and the array was operational by October 2025, with a monitoring portal and maintenance plan in place as of October 3. The expected electricity offset is still to be determined from the first months of monitoring data, which the report treats honestly as pending.
doe-osti-3364125-a-new-capability-for-in:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Greg A. Kimmel, Megan K. Dunlap, and Loni Kringle, dated May 2026, describes a new instrument setup for studying liquids under high pressure. The apparatus targets supercooled water, water chilled below its freezing point without turning to ice. Laser heating melts tiny ice samples in place, letting the team watch liquid structure and motion at pressures where ordinary containers and probes fail.

Design chapters work through crystallization times, heat flow times, and syringe sample handling, grounding each choice in estimates. Melting-rate analysis uses the Wilson-Frenkel model, with typical water diffusion values around 3 × 10-9 square meters per second. The capability opens experiments on how high pressure changes liquid behavior, a basic question for chemistry and planetary science alike.
doe-osti-3364614-fabrication-of-ceramic-:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Saumyadeep Jana, Jon L. Helgeland, Josef Matyas, and Devesh Chouhan, dated May 2026, tackles a joining problem at the heart of concentrating solar power receivers. Silicon carbide ceramic handles the receiver's high heat but must attach to structural metals such as 316L stainless steel. The two expand at very different rates, so a direct joint cracks under thermal stress.

The team built a graded interface that shifts composition step by step from ceramic to metal. Interlayer alloys were selected, tape-cast into thin stacks by a powder metallurgy route, and sintered until the layers bonded metallurgically. Coupons measuring 20 by 20 by 10 millimeters demonstrated the bond between reaction-bonded silicon carbide and steel. Mechanical tests and microscopy checked the joints. Graded transitions could let solar receivers run hotter and more efficiently.
doe-osti-3365610-artificial-intelligence:
A Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report dated September 2025 collects expert views on where the Office of International Nuclear Security should aim its artificial intelligence work. Jessica Baweja, Prashant Jain, and Alan Evans wrote it. In late fiscal 2025 the office formed an AI task force. It asked specialists what role the office could usefully play, given how many agencies now build AI tools.

Experts urged focus over breadth: pick specific domains such as perimeter intrusion detection, access control, alarm assessment, and insider threat detection, and serve them well. Rather than reviewing products one by one, the office should build evaluation methods partners can run themselves, map gaps between commercial tools and nuclear security needs, and design realistic tests. Detection comparisons need care, since true and false positive rates decide whether an alarm system is usable.
doe-osti-3366701-innovative-interfacial-:
Brown University's final report for DOE solar award DE-EE0009511 covers August 2021 to January 2025 work on perovskite solar cells. Nitin Padture led the project, with Kai Zhu and Joseph Berry among the collaborators. Perovskites promise cheap, efficient photovoltaics but degrade at their interfaces, where the light-absorbing layer meets charge-collecting contacts. The project engineered those interfaces to lift efficiency and stability together instead of trading one against another.

Self-assembled monolayer treatments and a fluorinated phenethylammonium iodide layer were combined on devices aged four days in the dark before measurement. Of 50 treated devices, 16 exceeded 21 percent power conversion efficiency. Charts of voltage, current, and fill factor document the spread, not just the champion cell. Interface chemistry, the results argue, is where perovskite durability will be won.
doe-osti-3372059-benchmarks-for-processi:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-26/21, by Braeton Smith, Nwike Iloeje, Rakesh Iyer, and co-authors, sets benchmarks for the plants that process, refine, and separate critical materials. Critical materials such as lithium and the rare earth elements feed batteries, magnets, and defense gear, yet most supply steps sit outside the United States. The team measured the current state of the art so that later process gains can be judged against a fixed yardstick.

The survey covers extraction, refining, separation, and recycling routes, drawn from published studies and talks with firms. One case follows acid-free dissolution of electronic waste, licensed to Critical Materials Recycling LLC, with a goal of 100 tonnes of high-purity rare earth oxides a year. The authors warn the benchmarks will shift as plants scale up.
doe-osti-3374112-digitally-optimized-aut:
Idaho National Laboratory slide deck INL/MIS-25-86924, dated August 2025, by Anthony Peter D'Andrea, Kaleb Houck, and Porter J. Zohner, presents a robotic system for handling waste tanks at Hanford. The project, backed by Hanford Tank Waste research funding, pairs Idaho engineers with a Florida International University team. Its near-term aim is checking tank pits without pulling off their heavy concrete caps, a costly job that also exposes workers.

The plan sends small robots through existing view ports only four inches wide, which caps the size of both platform and payload. A Ford Lightning electric truck serves as the deployment hub, housing the digital twin, autonomy, and data systems. Stress tests ran computers, motors, and a load bank off the truck's outlets; power stayed steady, with only small voltage dips when motors switched on.
doe-osti-3376512-integrated-security-saf:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-22860, printed in June 2026, is by Christopher Faucett, Alan Evans, and Ben Cipiti. It joins two questions often asked apart: what if a heat pipe reactor breaks, and what if someone breaks it. Heat pipe reactors cool their cores with pipes of working fluid, no pumps needed. The study runs one attack case through both lenses, so the fallout math stays the same on both sides.

The chain uses a five factor formula to set the source term. MELCOR then tracks the plant damage and the leak path out of the building. MACCS carries the plume to the public. One case prices a blast of surrogate burn gases. MELCOR puts their speed near 387 meters per second. At 150 pounds of gas, the motion energy lands near 4.98 megajoules. The report sets that beside the 4.184 megajoules from one kilogram of TNT.
doe-osti-3377904-stations-tool-for-autom:
The Stations Tool for Automated Permitting user manual, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5400-98402 from June 2026, teaches local officials to run S-TAP. S-TAP is a tool that automates permits for electric vehicle charging stations. Seven authors are printed, led by Erin Andrews-Sharer, Emily Dalecki, and Alexandria Danner. The manual is written for the authority having jurisdiction, the office that approves installations.

Setup is the heart of the walkthrough. The jurisdiction first picks which International Building Code and National Electrical Code cycle it has adopted. The permit form then adjusts itself to match. It then fills in general settings. It reviews the tool's built-in default standards against its own zoning and land use code. Where local codes give no standard, the jurisdiction may adopt its own or keep the defaults.
doe-osti-3377911-value-of-geothermal-ene:
Value of Geothermal Energy Storage for Supply-Side and Demand-Side Applications, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-6A40-95722 from June 2026, prices a simple idea. The idea is to use a geothermal reservoir itself as storage. The authors are Claire Halloran, Juliet Simpson, and Jonathan Ho. The study uses the laboratory's Cambium datasets, which model hourly futures for the United States electricity sector.

On the supply side, discharge duration was the strongest driver of value. Long-duration storage in an enhanced geothermal plant reservoir, at 20 hours of duration, had a regional median value of 470 dollars per kilowatt of plant capacity. That is more than double the value at five hours. That added value could cover 18 percent of a deep flash plant's capital costs under advanced 2050 cost projections. Most of it came from firm capacity rather than round-trip efficiency.
doe-osti-3383519-digital-grid-twin-direc:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4559, dated April 2026, builds a test bed inside a digital grid twin for one narrow question. How well do protective relays talk to each other directly? The authors are Emilio C. Piesciorovsky, Trupal Rajeshbhai Patel, and Matthew J. Reno, of the Electrification and Energy Infrastructures Division. Protective relays trip breakers to isolate faults. Their coordination depends on the communication link between them.

The test bed compares the two link types a utility might use, radio antennas and optical fiber. It compares them on performance and on misoperations, the failures where a relay acts wrongly or not at all. A digital twin lets the team stage faults and measure the links without risking real equipment. The report is the test bed's documentation: the direct communication scheme, the setup, and the assessment it was built to run.
doe-osti-3384916-ceramic-composite-exper:
Ceramic Composite Experimental Testing Status, Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4648 from June 2026, is a status account from the Materials Science and Technology Division. Six authors are printed: Josina W. Geringer, John Podhiny, Jiyoung Son, Melanie O'Connell, Zane Wallen, and Logan Kearney. Status reports of this kind freeze a testing program at a date so managers and sponsors can see what has been run and what remains.

Ceramic composites, fibers locked in a ceramic matrix, are tested to learn how they carry load and survive heat before they are trusted in service. The report's apparatus is a long list of figures and tables, the test evidence itself: specimen records, measured curves, and results to date. Readers looking for the program's current position, rather than a final verdict, are its audience.
doe-osti-3391368-integrated-simulation-o:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-93507, dated May 2026, integrates the simulation of weld residual stress and crack growth in one chain. Lynn Munday and Benjamin Spencer of Idaho wrote it with Tianchen Hu, Bipul Barua, and Cheng-Hau Yang of Argonne National Laboratory. The work belongs to the Nuclear Energy Advanced Modeling and Simulation program.

Welding locks stress into metal, and those stresses later drive cracks. The report documents capability built to follow both. It covers updates to a subdomain modifier, a birth strain treatment, and residual stress recovery. It also covers updates to XFEM, the extended finite element method that lets cracks grow through a mesh. Two examples exercise the chain. One is a simple plate weld simulation. The other is the J-groove weld of a control rod drive mechanism, a joint with a known cracking history in reactors.
doe-osti-3427088-an-educational-program-:
Northeastern University team Hameed Metghalchi, Yiannis Levendis, and Gregory Kowalski built an education program on concentrated solar power and heliostats. Their report, NLR/SR-6A42-100664, is dated August 2026. Heliostats are mirrors that track the sun and aim light at a tower.

Course units suit newcomers with technical training, policy analysts, and early researchers. Lessons cover solar radiation traits, storage needs, and solar field control. Running a field means managing many mirrors, not aligning one. Existing plant layouts and their limits get a full overview. The program trains staff for a niche but growing solar field.
doe-osti-3577313-advanced-research-on-in:
An energy study for Molokai, Hawaii is covered in National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5000-99722, dated August 2026. Five authors are printed on the title page: Jennifer King, Michael Ingram, Kumar Prabakar, Indu Manogaran, and Mahalia Hunt. The work came through the Energy to Communities Energyshed partnership. It used lab analysis tools to test ways to make the island grid tougher and more resilient.

Inside, the team sets out community goals, past and forecast power use, and load flow studies of the local grid. It compares mixes of solar, wind, batteries, hydrogen storage, and generators. Each mix is scored on cost and on how much clean power it can supply. One finding is that hydrogen storage grows more cost-effective when generators burn biodiesel, which costs more than diesel. The results give Molokai planners a grounded base for choosing system upgrades.
doe-osti-3683722-fusing-semantic-feature:
Sandia technical note SAND2026-25518R reports a way to sharpen three-dimensional maps built from satellite photos. Four team members are named: Albert W. Reed, Timothy Nagle-McNaughton, Shiloh N. Elliott, and Jesse P. Mapel. The work sits in the SMART project on semantic modelling for aerial reconstructions. Gaussian splatting, a leading rebuild method, leans only on colour images. Patchy light and flat, textureless ground in satellite views trip it up.

The team fused splatting with features from vision foundation models, which tag what each pixel shows. New steps compute features at several scales and align them across photos from different dates. On the IARPA 2019 challenge data, mean rebuild error fell by about five percent. Gains were largest in big flat areas, where colour matching is weakest. Textured scenes gained little. The best tested model was DINOv3.
doe-osti-3818506-resource-light-methods-: A single conference poster from a SULI intern session presents Joshua Willis's work with Trevor Martin and Nathan Neale at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Silicon nanoparticle anodes could hold ten times the charge of graphite, but their surfaces react with battery fluid. The poster compares surface treatments: a standard oxide coat, organic coats, lithium carbonate, a silicon-aluminum alloy shell, and a new house method. The house method gave the best capacity and charging efficiency while using fewer resources.
elements-of-civil-government-a-text-book:
Alexander L. Peterman, a Kentucky normal school principal and state senator, wrote a civics text for public schools, revised to 1916 and issued by the American Book Company. He dedicates the book to the teachers who train boys and girls in American citizenship. The preface states the method at once: begin at home.

The book starts with the family, the first government a child knows. It climbs through school, district, township, county, and state to the United States. Peterman calls the plan the simplest yet devised, built on the synthetic method he used for years in schools and institutes. Mid-text pages explain federal reserve banks and the commissioner of internal revenue, who gathers the income tax and the taxes on liquor and tobacco. Generations of schoolchildren learned their republic from this ladder.
giotto-and-his-works-in-padua-an-explana:
John Ruskin wrote this notice to explain a set of woodcuts made for the Arundel Society after Giotto's frescoes in the Arena Chapel at Padua. He says plainly that it is no history of Giotto's life; such a history would need long search in Italian libraries, for which he had no time. Instead he guides the reader through the pictures themselves.

Ruskin walks from scene to scene in the chapel, where Giotto painted the lives of Mary and of Christ on the walls. He points out the design, the feeling, and the faith in each fresco. His aim is to teach English readers how to look at early Italian art. The piece is short, intense, and full of Ruskin's forceful voice. It still serves as a doorway into one of the great painted rooms of Europe.
govdocs-archive_org-manual-of-zen-buddhi:
Daisetz Teitaro Suzuki, the scholar who introduced Zen Buddhism to the English-speaking world, compiled the Manual of Zen Buddhism as a handbook of the tradition's core texts. It gathers the scriptures and practice pieces a Zen student actually uses.

Inside are sutras, dharanis, hymns, and short writings, including texts used in daily monastery practice, in Suzuki's translations. The manual was many Western readers' first shelf of Zen in one volume. One caution: this scan's text layer is scrambled by a character-substitution cipher, so reading on screen is harder than the printed book deserves.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurgessDonaldPS:
On April 17, 1968, FBI Special Agent Donald P. Burgess inventoried what agents found in Room 2 at 113 14th Street NE. The search came thirteen days after the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., as the Bureau worked the case that became MURKIN.

The inventory lists small, odd items: key blanks, thread, a metal strip, and a card concealed behind door molding. Inventories like this one fix exactly what was seized and where, the foundation any later use of the evidence stands on. The document is preserved as filed, an evidence list from the King investigation's first weeks.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClineRayS_Cline:
Ray S. Cline ran the CIA's intelligence directorate and later directed the State Department's intelligence bureau, one of the analytic service's founding figures. This book-review section takes up his account of thirty years in the CIA, in a review by Vernon A. Guidry Jr.

The section reviews intelligence memoirs together, the shelf of insider accounts that grew through the exposure years as retired officers explained themselves in print. Guidry's judgments show how such books were received by reviewers who knew the world they described. The section is preserved as a sample of the era's intelligence literature being weighed in public.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBISolutiontoJF: An FBI memorandum dated November 22, 1966 is headed with the assassination of President John F. Kennedy. The date is exactly three years after the shooting in Dallas. The archived file is labeled by researchers as the Bureau's solution to the assassination. It gives no further detail in the surviving record. The memo stands as a dated headquarters paper on the case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LeikindSeymourS: A news article headlined 'Instructor's Apology Halts Charge' concerns Seymour S. Leikind, a teacher who faced a charge that ended after he apologized. The file preserves the headline and Leikind's name but no date, publication, or further detail. What can honestly be said is limited to that sequence: a charge existed, an apology was made, and the apology closed the matter, a small episode that someone clipped and kept.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MaloneWilliamSc:
William Scott Malone wrote 'The Secret Life of Jack Ruby' for New Times. Ruby, the Dallas nightclub owner, shot Lee Harvey Oswald on live television two days after the Kennedy assassination. Malone's article reports new evidence gathered by the House Select Committee on Assassinations about Ruby's activities and his connections to organized crime.

The committee's work in the late 1970s reopened questions the Warren Commission had closed. Ruby's phone calls, trips, and mob ties were examined again, witness by witness. Malone's piece brings that inquiry to magazine readers. It argues, through the committee's findings, that Ruby was less of a lone, grief-maddened man than the first account had made him.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartinezSotoJor: Special Agent James J. O'Connor of the FBI's Miami office wrote this report on April 3, 1964, concerning Jorge Antonio Martinez Soto. Miami agents handled the Cuban side of the Oswald inquiry, interviewing exiles and travelers who might have crossed Oswald's path. The file gives the agent, the office, the date, and the subject's name. It does not summarize O'Connor's findings, so the report's contents cannot be described beyond its place in that inquiry.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ThomasCarrollS_: Special Agent Love wrote up his interview with Carroll S. Thomas in an FBI memorandum dated March 16, 1967. Interview memos were the bureau's basic building blocks, turning a conversation into a dated, filed record. The Thomas memo belongs to the large body of paper the FBI produced while its field offices kept working assassination-related leads years after Dallas. It preserves one interview in the bureau's standard form.
govdocs-archive_org-spirit-man-nihal-ats: Spirit Man: Nihal Atsız's work - the made public government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated entry, filed, an obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner ends his westward march on the Pacific Slope. The Voyager of Whulge opens the volume in the Northwest. Skinner says the Siwash give every tree a soul. Forests hold good and evil spirits who get due offerings.

Mountain spirits, called tamanouses, fight in fire and stone, he tells. Tacoma and Hood hurled rocks that dammed the Columbia. Gold-rush ghosts and Spanish mission tales fill later pages. Death Valley's queen and Bridal Veil Fall close the list. The newest-settled coast was already thick with legend, and Skinner caught it while the tales were young.
nasa-tm-19650025681-a-new-series-of-nick:
John C Freche and William J Waters at Lewis Research Center introduced a new series of nickel-base alloys built for service above eighteen hundred degrees Fahrenheit. Their article was prepared for a foundry magazine. It covers how the alloys are melted and cast, a step that decides much of their quality. Strength, ductility, and resistance to oxidation are all reported.

Hot engine parts need metals that keep strength without wasting away in hot gas. Nickel alloys were the leading choice for that duty. A new series had to prove itself in casting as well as in service. Freche and Waters also cover the metallurgy behind the gains, for readers who cast such parts.
nasa-tm-19670030985-solar-sails-a-realis:
Sunlight pushes on things, and Mgr. Urbanczyk builds a case for sailing on that push. His article first appeared in Polish in the journal Astronautyka in 1965. The English translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, in August 1967, arguing that solar sails are realistic spacecraft propulsion.

The article opens with comet tails, the oldest visible proof of light pressure. A comet's tail swings around as the comet rounds the Sun, defying gravity. Galileo, Kepler, and Newton all puzzled over that reversal. Solar radiation, blowing outward in all directions, is the force that compels the tail to turn.
nasa-tm-19680009886-lunar-solar-perturba:
B. K. Martynenko wrote this orbit study in Russian, published in 1967 in a Soviet theoretical astronomy bulletin. The translation was issued at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, on December 28, 1967. It analyzes how the Moon and Sun tug on a satellite whose orbit takes just under a day.

Two test satellites are compared. One circles in the equatorial plane; the other flies in a plane standing upright to Earth's orbit path. The first satellite's perigee is tuned to quiet the tugs' long-term effect. Its orbit proves stable, its ovalness slowly shrinking. The second orbit, tuned for maximum effect, grows more oval fast enough to limit its lifetime.
nasa-tm-19680017998-applications-of-comp:
Richard R. Heldenfels of Langley Research Center reviews filamentary composites for space vehicle structures in this paper, presented in May 1967. Such materials embed strong fibers in a lighter matrix. They promise lower structural mass than metals alone, a major gain for spacecraft.

Heldenfels compares composite properties with the design needs of vehicles used in space operations. He identifies many potential uses across space vehicles. Few of those uses had been made or even planned at the time. Wider use awaited solutions in analysis, design, fabrication, and reliability. The review maps both the promise and the work still needed. It remains a snapshot of composites at an early stage.
nasa-tm-19690019017-preliminary-soil-cla: A preliminary soil classification map of the southwestern United States and Mexico, dated May 1968, was produced by the U.S. Geological Survey from space photography. The report record states the photography came from the Gemini 4 and Gemini 5 missions. Mapping soils from orbit tests whether spacecraft pictures can serve Earth science. The hosted sample preserves only a document release form for the map, with no readable map or explanation. No soil classes or regions can therefore be described from the sample beyond the stated origin.
nasa-tm-19690026086-an-effective-automat:
R. J. Stattel, P. L. Hinds, and G. U. Bell of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this March 1969 preprint, X-721-69-70. As an ADP feasibility study, it designs an effective automatic data processing system for sounding rocket telemetry. Rockets return brief bursts of PPM and PCM data, two pulse formats the ground system must digest quickly and well.

The study first examines pulse position modulation and the present processing system, weighing its advantages and limits. It then lays out a proposed replacement, from a basic plan to an ultimate system. Size and speed needs are considered, and alternate plans are tested for feasibility. Conclusions and a summary of management and procurement considerations close the study for decision makers.
nasa-tm-19690026385-the-improvement-of-a:
John P. Quitter of Lewis Research Center and J. W. Schaelchlin of General Dynamics Convair report upgrading an electronic power supply in this report, NASA TM X-1875. The component is an inverter supplying three-phase, 400-hertz power to the Centaur space vehicle. Early ground failures and design flaws drew heavy engineering attention to it.

The program upgraded every piece part used in the inverter. Mechanical and thermal design were also improved. Quitter describes weaknesses found in the original parts. He then presents the reasoning behind each better replacement choice. Serious design obstacles were overcome along the way. The result was a highly reliable component fit for space use.
nasa-tm-19700001295-evaluation-testing-o:
Evaluation Testing of Thermofit Solder Sleeves is a Quality and Reliability Assurance Laboratory report, numbered 53968 and dated November 1969. Thermofit sleeves join wires in one heating step, shrinking tight while their solder melts inside. The tests judge whether such joints meet aerospace reliability needs on two wire types.

The sleeve model D-101-31 was tested on nickel clad copper wire and alloy wire. Checks covered voltage drop, peel strength, dielectric strength, water immersion, and moisture resistance. High temperature aging and vibration trials followed. One trial sought the heating time giving the strongest joint. Prefluxing the shield braid gave very good wetting, the testers found, but left a corrosive flux residue behind.
nasa-tm-19700009636-preliminary-evaluati:
James S. Fear of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1969. It tests a new kind of liner for a turbojet combustor, the chamber where fuel burns. The liner wall was a perforated sheet cooled by a film of air.

Fear compared that liner with the standard stepped slot design in the same combustor. Both burners used the same jet fuel in tests near normal air pressure. The sheet liner did its job well, the report states. It caused no harm to burning efficiency, pressure loss, or the pattern of exit temperatures.
nasa-tm-19700011350-a-simplified-dead-re:
Walter L. Green of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on September 30, 1969. It presents a simple navigation system for the manned lunar roving vehicle. Dead reckoning means keeping track of position by logging each move from a known start point.

The basic hardware for Green's system is two free gyroscopes, the abstract states. A gyroscope that spins freely can hold a steady direction reference as the vehicle moves. The report sets out the system for use by astronauts driving on the Moon. It aimed to give crews a clear way to know where they were on the surface.
nasa-tm-19700018806-communication-for-th:
The Scientific and Technical Information Division at the Marshall Space Flight Center compiled this volume on December 12, 1969. Communication for the 70's gathers talks from a Huntsville seminar held the October before. The speakers were technical writers, artists, and other specialists who explain science and engineering for a living.

The papers appear in the order they were given, with no attempt to blend them into one argument. Talks cover graphic arts, the work of the technical artist, and the designer as communicator. Others trace the rise of the professional communicator and take apart what makes a good presentation. A short preface says the point throughout is how much clear communication matters in technical fields.
nasa-tm-19700021221-discrete-control-of-:
Jeremiah F. Creedon wrote this doctoral thesis at the University of Rhode Island in 1970. It develops discrete control methods for linear distributed systems. The test case is the flexible main mirror of a large telescope in orbit.

A big mirror in space bends slightly under heat and motion. To keep images sharp, its surface must hold a near-perfect shape. Creedon's method adjusts the mirror at set points and set times, rather than smoothly. His work tackles one of the hard problems of orbiting astronomy. Mirrors that correct themselves could give telescopes sharper views than rigid mirrors allow.
nasa-tm-19700026656-thermal-evaluation-o:
The Thermal Technology Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this working paper on September 8, 1969. It evaluates heater models for the early Apollo science packages left on the Moon. The heaters used isotopes, and their warmth kept instruments alive through the cold lunar night.

Tests ran in the center's arc-heated facility, which can mimic fierce heating. The paper describes the test models and the test gear. It then gives the test conditions and the steps that were followed. Results and a discussion close the main text, followed by final remarks. Such checks made sure the heaters would work on the Moon.
nasa-tm-19700027279-space-transportation:
NASA held this technology symposium at the Lewis Research Center on July 15 to 17, 1970. It covered the coming Space Transportation System, the shuttle program then taking shape. The papers came out in seven volumes, one for each technical area.

Volume Two covers dynamics and aeroelasticity. Its topics are dynamic loads and response, aeroelasticity itself, and flight dynamics and environment. A hybrid craft that is both airplane and launch vehicle strains both fields at once. Specialists used the meeting to share problems and early answers. The set of volumes forms a snapshot of shuttle science at the start of the program.
nasa-tm-19700033660-space-transportation:
NASA held this technology symposium at the Lewis Research Center on July 15 to 17, 1970. It covered the coming Space Transportation System, the shuttle program then taking shape. The papers came out in seven volumes, one for each technical area.

Volume Three covers structures and materials. Its topics are materials technology, thermal protection systems, and structural design technology. A reusable craft must stand launch loads and fierce reentry heat, then fly again. The papers share early work on airframes, heat shields, and the metals and tiles behind them. The volumes form a snapshot of shuttle science at the program's start.
nasa-tm-19710011822-goddard-range-and-ra:
J. G. Marsh, B. C. Douglas, and S. M. Klosko of the Goddard Space Flight Center issued this preprint in January 1971, numbered X-552-71-52. They used observations of the GEOS-2 satellite to fix the exact positions of tracking stations on Earth's surface. The stations included three laser sites and four Goddard range and range rate sites.

Their method combined optical, laser, and range-rate tracking in dynamic orbit solutions tied to Earth's center of mass. The abstract reports accuracy of about ten meters or better for most stations. Distances between sites matched the quality expected of first-order ground surveys. The authors also found that the combined solutions supported the gravity value the Jet Propulsion Laboratory had derived from deep space tracking.
nasa-tm-19710016135-a-conceptual-study-o:
W. N. Redisch, A. F. White, and G. Goldberg of the Goddard Space Flight Center directed this conceptual study, published in January 1971. It designs a geostationary satellite that would serve aircraft over the oceans. A spinning momentum wheel would hold the satellite steady while it kept a fixed aim related to the Sun.

The design work itself was done by Fairchild-Hiller's Space and Electronics Systems Division under a NASA contract. The satellite was meant for a planned NASA and European experimental aeronautical system over oceanic regions. The authors warn that the results are preliminary and that some points, like the L-band antenna design, need more work. Even so, the report concludes that the satellite is feasible within the mission guidelines, with margin for weight growth.
nasa-tm-19720004252-aerodynamic-characte:
Michael D Falarski and David G Koenig reported large model tests in July 1971, as NASA TM X-62,029. Both worked at Moffett Field, for the Ames Research Center and the Army Air Mobility laboratory. Their model joined a swept wing with an augmented jet flap. Blowing air through the flap boosts lift for slow flight. The tests ran in the huge forty by eighty foot wind tunnel.

The data cover the model's lengthwise behavior in detail. Runs were made with and without a horizontal tail fitted. Early results on sidewise and directional behavior are also included. Big models in a big tunnel give readings close to full scale flight. Such data guided work on short takeoff transports.
nasa-tm-19720015149-comparison-of-the-ef:
George W Lewis Jr and Donald C Urasek of the Lewis Research Center compared blade dampers in April 1972, as NASA TM X-2536. Their test rotor was a twenty inch axial flow transonic compressor rotor. Small dampers fitted between blades kept vibration in check. The same rotor had run earlier with dampers twice as large. That history allowed a clean size comparison on identical hardware, a rare chance in compressor research.

The small dampers lost less energy in their region. Local heat rise and pressure ratio there ran higher as a result. Overall efficiency and pressure ratio barely changed, though. At design speed, the small damper rotor held a greater stall margin. At lower speeds, the large damper rotor kept a wider flow range.
nasa-tm-19720016239-the-ultraviolet-flux:
A NASA astronomy preprint from Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, presents ultraviolet flux envelopes of main-sequence B stars. Its author names are not legible in the scan. It presents energy curves for hot blue stars on an absolute scale, spanning wavelengths from the ultraviolet into visible light. Such curves tell astronomers how much light a star emits at each color.

The envelopes were built from OAO-2 satellite scans and published ground-based material, with rocket scans for Sirius. Stars covered include gamma Leporis, eta Ursae Majoris, gamma Ursae Majoris, and alpha Lyrae. The key finding is heavy line blocking at short wavelengths, cutting the light by as much as half at the shortest wavelengths measured. Stars with nearly identical visible spectra proved to differ in the ultraviolet. So a ground-based spectral type does not precisely predict a star's ultraviolet output.
our-nig-or-sketches-from-the-life-of-a-f:
Harriet E. Wilson published Our Nig in 1859. It tells of a free Black girl indentured in a white household in the North. Her subtitle insists the sketches show that slavery's shadows fall even there. In her preface Wilson confesses she cannot minister to refined readers as abler pens do. Deserted by kindred and disabled by failing health, she writes to maintain herself and her child, and she pointedly refuses to soften slavery's northern face to spare anyone's feelings.

Her mistress, she says, was wholly imbued with southern principles, and she has omitted what would most provoke shame in good anti-slavery friends at home. The book, the first novel published by an African American woman, vanished for over a century before scholars restored it to its place in American letters.
pictures-every-child-should-know-a-selec:
Pictures Every Child Should Know selects the world's art masterpieces for young people. The title page gives the author as Dolores Bacon, and an introduction begins the teaching at art's beginning. Man's wish to decorate his belongings, it says, is among the earliest signs of civilisation, from lines indented in clay onward.

The introduction moves from Egyptian drawing to Indian pottery and the working of metals in America, in plain language for children. Bacon quotes many authoritative writers on artists and pictures. The aim is to give young readers the great paintings of the world, with the stories and looking-skills to make them their own.
podcast-dannyjones-M1EK3lTTd-s:
The guest called Esoteric Eddie joins Danny Jones to argue an arresting thesis. He holds that the Bible itself proves Satan was an alien. In his reading, Satan was a being from elsewhere, misread by believers as a purely spiritual enemy. His case runs through the ancient texts describing fallen beings who came down to earth.

Eddie reads Genesis and the Book of Enoch beside modern UFO reports, treating the ancient astronaut framework as a translation key. Jones follows the verses and asks where translation ends and invention begins. The claim is Eddie's, well outside any scholarly or church consensus, and it is kept here as he states it. Listeners drawn to the alien reading of scripture get one of its younger advocates making the full case, text by text, in the conversational format where the theory now lives.
podcast-joerogan-UL3RvjhFu_s:
Activist Shannon O'Loughlin joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1442 to talk about Native issues. O'Loughlin leads a national group for Native arts and cultures and has worked as a lawyer for tribal causes. Her visit brings policy and history into a studio that rarely hosts either.

She and Rogan discuss tribal rights, the return of remains and sacred objects, and how federal law still shapes Native life. Rogan asks the basic questions many listeners share, and O'Loughlin answers from case work. The episode is a grounded, informative hour on subjects the show usually meets only in passing.
rupert-of-hentzau-from-the-memoirs-of-fr:
Anthony Hope wrote Rupert of Hentzau as a sequel to The Prisoner of Zenda, told from the memoirs of Fritz von Tarlenheim. The contents list twenty-one chapters, from The Queen's Good-By and A Station Without a Cab to Again to Zenda and An Audience of the King. Later titles include The King in Strelsau, What the Chancellor's Wife Saw, Young Rupert and the Play-Actor, and The Triumph of the King. The closing chapters are headed For Our Love and Her Honor, The Decision of Heaven, and The Coming of the Dream.

Chapter I opens with Fritz musing that each act, however light, may breed results that spread far and flow for years. He asks whether the death of the Duke of Strelsau and the freeing of King Rudolf should not end the troubles born of Black Michael's bold plot.
six-little-bunkers-at-cousin-tom-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book in her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. A front picture shows the young travelers steaming down past the Statue of Liberty. The pages at hand show the title page plus lists of Hope's many series, among them the Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown books, priced at fifty cents a volume. No chapter text appears in these opening pages, so the six children's visit to Cousin Tom cannot be told from what is shown here.
six-little-bunkers-at-grandma-bell-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book as an early volume of her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. The pages at hand show the title page plus lists of the series and of Hope's Bobbsey Twins books, which run from the twins at home to a great city. No chapter text appears in these opening pages. The six children's stay at Grandma Bell's, and what befell them there, cannot be told fairly from the front pages alone.
six-little-bunkers-at-grandpa-ford-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book in her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. A front picture shows Laddie crying that the children got someone up but cannot get him down. The pages at hand show the title page plus the series list, with volumes at Grandma Bell's, Aunt Jo's, and Cousin Tom's. No chapter text appears in these opening pages, so the fun and trouble at Grandpa Ford's cannot be told from what is shown here.
six-little-bunkers-at-mammy-june-s: Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book in her Six Little Bunkers series, issued in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures by Walter S. Rogers. The series list at the front runs to eight volumes, ending with this visit to Mammy June. The pages at hand show the title page plus lists of Hope's Bobbsey Twins and other series. No chapter text appears in these opening pages, so what the six children found at Mammy June's cannot be told fairly from the front pages alone.
snow-bound-at-eagle-s:
Bret Harte opens Snow-Bound at Eagle's with a stage-coach climbing through dark and hush toward a Sierra summit. The coach sways on its straps with so faint a link to the unseen horses that it seems to glide by some hid force. Tall tree trunks drift past the windows like ghosts, and pine needles choke the road and deaden all sound.

The coach halts without warning. Three riders wake at once, but the fourth, John Hale, has not slept and turns to the window in haste. What looked like trees stands still outside, and one shape proves to be a man with a gun at the window. A voice in the dark orders the riders down, and a second voice snaps at a man whose hand moved behind him.
tales-of-st-austin-s:
P. G. Wodehouse published Tales of St Austin's in 1903, his early set of school stories, most first printed in The Captain and the Public School Magazine. Twelve tales are listed, from How Pillingshot Scored and The Odd Trick to The Prize Poem.

Wodehouse notes in his short preface that one tale, A Shocking Affair, appears in print for the first time. The tales follow boys at a boarding school through games, tricks, scrapes, and small wins. Readers get the light touch and neat plots that later made Wodehouse famed, here in a young form aimed at school life and boyish pride.
the-canadian-elocutionist-designed-for-t:
The Canadian Elocutionist, by Anna K. Howard, was designed for the use of colleges, schools, and self-instruction, and offers selections in prose and poetry for reading and recitation. A motto from Chesterfield heads the book, and the title page identifies its compiler as a teacher of elocution, Miss Anna Halleck Kelsey, holding the LL.B.

Her preface was written at Toronto on September 24, 1885. It states her method plainly. She would simplify the rules of the art and avoid abstruse terms. She presents the system of instruction she had used with success in her own practice. The work is a practical manual of delivery, built by a working teacher for students who needed rules they could actually apply.
the-girl-from-keller-s:
Harold Bindloss wrote The Girl from Keller's. Frederick A. Stokes Company printed it in New York in 1917. In England it came out as Sadie's Conquest. Chapter I is called The Portrait. It opens at dusk on the Saskatchewan prairie. Festing stops by a ravine near a half-built railroad bridge.

Festing has just learned hard news. A post he thought was his has gone to another man. He looks back at the blast lamps on the bridge. He looks ahead at the still, empty grass. He knows the railroad will soon fill the waste with wheat farms. He feels his own life has reached a fork. He must now choose a new path.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, in the version published in 1913 by the C. & G. Merriam Co. of Springfield, Mass., under the direction of Noah Porter, is a full guide to English spelling and meaning. The portion here covers the letter S. A long opening note explains the sounds of the letter, from a plain hiss to the voiced sound heard in wise, and its place in the ending -s.

Entries then explain the plural ending, the verb ending, and the possessive form before the main word list begins. Early headwords include Saadh, Saan, and Sabadilla, a Mexican plant once used in medicine. Each entry gives origin, pronunciation, and use, with marks for old, rare, or local senses.
the-head-of-kay-s: P. G. Wodehouse wrote The Head of Kay's. The record is dated 1905. The contents list eighteen chapters. Early titles include Mainly About Fenn and An Evening at Kay's. Later titles include The Final House-Match and Camp. One chapter is called The Raid on the Guard-Tent. Another is called The Dethronement of Fenn. The record present here holds front matter only. The school story itself does not appear.
the-investment-of-influence-a-study-of-s:
Newell Dwight Hillis wrote this study of social sympathy and service. Fleming H. Revell issued this edition in 1912. Copyright dates from 1897. His earlier books include A Man's Value to Society. The dedication addresses an unnamed friend simply as you. That friend guided him for many years. Friendship doubled his joys and halved his sorrows. It strengthened him where he was weak. It weakened him where he was too strong. The book teaches in precept what the friend taught in example.

His foreword states the turn he wants. Our fathers stressed self-care and self-culture. A man who made the most of himself served others best. Hillis turns that old gospel outward. Influence becomes a kind of capital. It is to be invested in other people, not hoarded. Hillis was a prominent Brooklyn preacher. The book carries a pulpit voice into social ethics.
the-jester-of-st-timothy-s: Arthur Stanwood Pier wrote this novel. The pages present here hold only a scouts leaf. None of the story itself appears. The leaf lists honorary officers of the Boy Scouts of America. Woodrow Wilson served as honorary president. William H. Taft and Theodore Roosevelt were the honorary vice-presidents. Ernest Thompson Seton was chief scout. Daniel Carter Beard was national scout commissioner. Nothing of St. Timothy's School or its jester can be read here. The wrapper swallowed the tale.
the-man-from-brodney-s: George Barr McCutcheon, author of Graustark and Brewster's Millions, wrote The Man from Brodney's, dated 1908 with illustrations by Harrison Fisher. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The twenty-four chapters shown begin with The Late Mr. Skaggs and An Extraordinary Document. They introduce Hollingsworth Chase, then promise The English Invade, The Château, The Brownes Arrive, and the title chapter itself. The Burning of the Bungalow, The Plague Is Announced, and The Charity Ball follow.
the-outdoor-girls-in-a-motor-car-or-the-: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls in a Motor Car, or The Haunted Mansion of Shadow Valley. Grosset and Dunlap published it in New York. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The lists name the Outdoor Girls of Deepdale and at Rainbow Lake before this volume. Winter Camp and Florida come next. Hope's Bobbsey Twins books are listed below, each at 50 cents postpaid.
the-poetical-works-of-addison-gay-s-fabl: The Poetical Works of Joseph Addison, bound with Gay's Fables and Somerville's Chase, was issued in 1859 with memoirs and critical dissertations by the Reverend George Gilfillan. Here only the title page and the start of the contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The Addison contents list a life of the poet, then poems on several occasions. They include a piece to Mr. Dryden, a poem to his Majesty, and a translation of Virgil's fourth Georgic without the story of Aristaeus. Odes for St. Cecilia's Day also appear.
the-rector-of-st-mark-s:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes, author of Lena Rivers and other popular novels, opens on a Friday afternoon with young rector Arthur Leighton finishing his Sunday sermon. Leighton turns gladly to a south window where June roses peer in, relieved that the week's work is done.

Holmes insists her rector remains a man, conscientious about souls yet eager that listeners admire both his teaching and its form, and still capable of love despite prayer and struggle against it. That tension between pulpit duty and human feeling drives the novel. Readers of domestic fiction will find a clerical hero treated with sympathy rather than satire.
the-sequel-of-appomattox-a-chronicle-of-: Walter Lynwood Fleming wrote The Sequel of Appomattox, a chronicle of the reunion of the states. It is volume thirty-two of the Chronicles of America series, in a textbook edition. Yale University Press published it in 1919. The pages shown give the title matter and a full contents list only. The text stops at the book's title heading. Chapters treat the aftermath of war and the work of the presidents. The trial of President Johnson and the Ku Klux movement appear. Restoration of home rule closes the list.
the-thin-santa-claus-the-chicken-yard-th:
Ellis Parker Butler's Thin Santa Claus, published by Doubleday, Page in 1909 with pictures by May Wilson Preston, carries the subtitle The Chicken Yard That Was a Christmas Stocking. It opens on a gray, drizzling Christmas morning with Mrs. Gratz in bed by the window. She rolls over, pulls the shade aside, and looks out at the weather. The frontispiece shows her watching a thin man search her chicken yard for 'toober-chlosis bugs.'

Another picture caption says the thin man looked like someone who had lost nine hundred dollars, not like Santa Claus. Butler, a beloved American humorist, builds his Christmas tale from that odd search. Readers get a widow, a mysterious skinny visitor, and a holiday mystery played for warmth and laughs from the very first page.
the-three-bronte-s: May Sinclair's Three Brontës, dated 1912, opens in this record with her prefatory note of thanks and a contents heading, but no critical prose beyond that. Sinclair thanks Clement K. Shorter for placing his copyright material at her disposal. She also acknowledges permission to draw heavily on Emily Brontë's poems in the Dodd, Mead edition of 1902 and in Shorter's Complete Poems. Alfred Sutro and Arthur Symons lent translations. The study of Charlotte, Emily, and Anne that made Sinclair's early reputation begins past the pages shown here.
the-young-gentleman-and-lady-s-monitor-a:
J. Hamilton Moore compiled The Young Gentleman and Lady's Monitor in an edition dated 1802. The title page promises select pieces from the best modern writers. Its aims include eradicating vulgar prejudices and rusticity of manners. Reading, writing, and speaking English elegantly are the goals. Schools, academies, and private readers are all addressed. Portions are sized for reading aloud in classes.

Moore's preface defines learning's design in elevated terms. Learning should make people agreeable companions to themselves. It should also make them useful members of society. Solitude and temptation alike require its discipline, he argues. The anthology thus teaches manners and morals together. Such monitors shaped polite education in the early republic.
